FEMA · Overseas investment · 2026

# Own a US LLC but never filed Form FC? Here is how to fix it

Thousands of Indian freelancers, agencies and founders formed a US LLC online, often for Stripe or US clients, and never told their Indian bank. No capital was sent, so it didn’t feel like an investment. Under FEMA it usually is. The good news: this is fixable, and fixing it before someone asks is much cheaper than after.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Fix your LLC reporting
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Owning a US LLC is ODI, even if only formation fees were paid by card.
- File Form FC for a UIN, then missed APRs; late submission fee within the window, compounding beyond.
- Sort the tax side too: Schedule FA, how LLC income is shown, transfer pricing.

Quick answer: an Indian resident who owns a foreign LLC has made an overseas direct investment, even if only formation fees were paid by card. Report it on Form FC through your bank to get a UIN, file the missed APRs, and pay a late submission fee if the delay is within the window the rules allow; otherwise apply for compounding. Then line up the tax side: Schedule FA, how the LLC’s income is shown, and transfer pricing.

## Why it counts as an overseas investment

- Owning shares or membership interest in a foreign entity is overseas investment under FEMA, whatever the amount.

- Paying formation or registered-agent fees personally can still be treated as funding the LLC.

- Resident individuals can only invest in an operating foreign entity (not one doing financial services), so check the LLC’s activity too.

- Full rules: FEMA and ODI rules when Indians own a US company.

## The fix, step by step

- Map the timeline: formation date, every payment to or for the LLC, bank account opening, and income received.

- Form FC and UIN: file Form FC through your AD bank with the LLC documents and valuation; the bank reports it to RBI and you get a Unique Identification Number.

- Late submission fee or compounding: delayed reports filed within the period the rules allow can be regularised with a late submission fee. Delays beyond that, or other contraventions, go through compounding, now handled by RBI regional offices for many ODI cases.

- Missed APRs: file an Annual Performance Report for each year, due 31 December, based on the LLC’s financial statements.

- The audit question: as the sole owner you control the LLC, so the APR generally needs audited financial statements even if US law does not require an audit. See APR and audit rules.

Until reporting is regularised, your bank may refuse further remittances to the LLC.

## The tax side (don’t skip it)

- Schedule FA: the LLC interest and its US bank account belong in Schedule FA of every resident return. Missing it can cost ₹10 lakh per year under the Black Money Act once foreign assets cross ₹20 lakh. FAST-DS is open until 31 December 2026 for past omissions.

- How the income is shown: a single-member LLC is ignored for US federal tax, but for Indian purposes it is usually treated as a separate foreign company. Showing the LLC’s receipts as your own turnover, or the reverse, needs to be thought through and kept consistent.

- Transfer pricing: you and your LLC are associated enterprises. If you transact with it (services, fees, funds), those can be international transactions needing an arm’s-length price and a report in Form 3CEB (Form 48 from tax year 2026-27).

- US filings: a foreign-owned single-member LLC files a pro forma Form 1120 with Form 5472 each year. Keep that consistent with your Indian filings.

## Documents to gather

- Articles of organisation, EIN letter, operating agreement

- US bank statements since opening

- Card or bank statements for formation and running costs paid from India

- US filings (1120 and 5472), and your Indian returns for the same years

- Any correspondence with your bank about the LLC

## Sources

- RBI: Master Direction, Overseas Investment
- IRS: Form 5472 for foreign-owned single-member LLCs

## Frequently asked questions
Do I need Form FC if I formed a US LLC without sending money from India?
Usually yes. Owning a foreign LLC is an overseas direct investment under FEMA even if only formation fees were paid by card. Form FC is filed through your AD bank to get a UIN, followed by Annual Performance Reports.

Late submission fee or compounding for a US LLC set up without Form FC?
Delayed reports filed within the period the overseas investment rules allow can usually be regularised with a late submission fee. Longer delays and other contraventions need compounding with the RBI. The answer depends on your exact dates, so map the timeline first.

Does a single-member US LLC need an audit for the APR?
Generally yes. Unaudited, certified statements are accepted only where the Indian investor has no control and the host country does not require an audit. As the sole member, you control the LLC, so audited statements are normally needed for the APR.

Does transfer pricing apply between me and my US LLC?
It can. An individual and the foreign entity they own are associated enterprises, so services, fees or funds between you can be international transactions requiring an arm's-length price and a Form 3CEB report (Form 48 from tax year 2026-27).

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Due diligence in India

# Due diligence in India for French companies

French groups are adding Indian suppliers, partners and subsidiaries. French law already asks large companies to evaluate their third parties: Sapin II for corruption risk and the duty of vigilance for human rights and environmental risk. We check Indian counterparties on the ground and report in English, in a form your compliance team can file.

Discuss your Indian partner
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Sapin II: evaluate Indian suppliers and intermediaries according to your risk map.
- Duty of vigilance: cover Indian subcontractors and suppliers in the vigilance plan.
- India–France treaty: generally 10% on dividends, interest, royalties; MFN needs notification.

## Why companies from here use us

- French industrial, aerospace, energy, luxury and technology groups keep adding Indian suppliers and partners.

- Sapin II and duty-of-vigilance files need documented, verifiable findings on third parties, not just a questionnaire the partner fills in.

- India is 3.5 to 4.5 hours ahead of France, so calls fit comfortably in the French working day.

## Your home-country rules — and what they mean for an Indian partner

- Sapin II (law of 9 December 2016): companies with at least 500 employees and turnover above €100 million (including on a group basis) must run an anti-corruption programme. One of its pillars is the evaluation of third parties: customers, first-tier suppliers and intermediaries, according to the risk map. The AFA checks these programmes.

- Duty of vigilance (law of 27 March 2017): companies with at least 5,000 employees in France, or 10,000 worldwide, publish a vigilance plan covering serious risks to human rights, health and safety and the environment in their own operations, subsidiaries, and subcontractors and suppliers they have an established relationship with.

- EU rules coming: the EU due diligence directive (CSDDD) will apply from 2029 after national transposition.

- What that means in India: documented checks on Indian agents, distributors, customs brokers and suppliers: who owns them, government links, how intermediaries are paid, and labour and environmental practices on site. See supplier verification and India’s anti-bribery law.

## The India side

- India–France tax treaty: Indian tax on dividends, interest, royalties and fees for technical services is generally limited to 10%. The “most favoured nation” clause does not apply automatically: India’s Supreme Court held in 2023 (Nestlé SA) that it needs a separate notification.

- Setting up in India: the resident director rule · India entry · start with an India Company Check on one company.

- Brands entering India: franchise, licence or own stores. Exporting to the EU: EUDR and CBAM data from Indian suppliers.

- In French: page en français. Planning India? Book a free 15-minute call.

## What we check for you in India

- Identity, registrations and filed financial statements of the Indian partner — how it works.

- Financial, tax and FEMA review; related parties; litigation through public records and counsel.

- Promoters, directors, government links and how intermediaries are paid — for your anti-bribery and supply-chain files.

- Premises visits from Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Rajkot or Dubai, with a written report in English.

- Full scope: partner due diligence · investment due diligence · supplier verification.

We are Chartered Accountants, not lawyers: home-country legal advice on compliance programmes stays with your counsel. Our reports are built to slot into their files.

## Sources

- Legifrance: Loi n° 2016-1691 (Sapin II)
- Legifrance: Loi n° 2017-399 (devoir de vigilance)
- Agence française anticorruption (AFA)

## Frequently asked questions
Who can do due diligence on an Indian company for a French company?
CA Durgesh Chavda's team checks Indian partners, suppliers and targets for French companies: records, financials, tax, FEMA, ownership, promoters, government links and premises, with a written report in English suited to Sapin II and duty-of-vigilance files.

Does Sapin II require due diligence on Indian suppliers?
For companies in scope (at least 500 employees and over EUR 100 million turnover), Sapin II requires evaluating third parties such as first-tier suppliers and intermediaries according to the risk map. Indian suppliers and agents in higher-risk categories need documented checks.

What is the withholding tax on royalties from India to France?
Under the India–France tax treaty, Indian tax on royalties and fees for technical services is generally 10%, provided the French company gives a tax residency certificate and the required declaration. The treaty's most favoured nation clause needs a separate Indian notification to apply.

India entry · Brands and retail · 2026

# Bringing your brand to India: franchise, licence, JV or your own stores

Foreign brands enter India in four main ways: a master franchise, a licence, a joint venture, or their own subsidiary running stores. Each has different FDI rules, tax on the money you take out, and a different level of risk sitting with your Indian partner.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Plan your India entry
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Franchise or licence: no FDI approval; royalty taxed at 20% or the treaty rate.
- Own stores: single-brand retail, 100% automatic; 30% India sourcing above 51% FDI.
- The Indian partner is the biggest risk: check finances, promoters, track record, related parties.

Quick answer: franchising and licensing need no FDI approval; you earn royalties, taxed in India at 20% (plus surcharge and cess) or the lower treaty rate. Owning stores yourself is single-brand retail: 100% FDI under the automatic route, but above 51% you must source 30% of goods from India. Whatever the route, the Indian partner is the biggest risk, so check them properly.

## The four routes compared

Route | Your investment | How you earn | Control | 

Master franchise | None | Upfront fee and royalties | Through the franchise agreement and brand standards | 

Licensing (brand or technology) | None | Royalties | Limited to the licence terms | 

Joint venture | Equity in an Indian company | Dividends, plus royalties if licensed | Shared, set by the shareholders’ agreement | 

Own subsidiary (single-brand retail) | Full | Retail profits | Full | 

## FDI rules if you own the stores

- Single-brand retail trading: up to 100% FDI under the automatic route, for products sold under one brand.

- Local sourcing: above 51% FDI, at least 30% of the value of goods bought must come from India, measured as an average over the first five years from the first store, then every year.

- Online first: you can sell online before opening physical stores, but are expected to open stores within two years.

- Multi-brand retail is far more restricted: up to 51% with government approval and conditions.

- Investors with Chinese or other land-border owners: see Press Note 2 (2026).

## Tax on royalties and fees

- Withholding tax: the Indian partner deducts tax on royalties and technical fees paid to you: 20% plus surcharge and cess under Indian law, or the lower treaty rate (often 10% to 15%) if you provide a tax residency certificate and the self-declaration in Form 41.

- No RBI approval is needed to pay royalties; they are current-account payments, made through the partner’s bank with the usual tax forms.

- GST: the Indian partner pays GST on imported royalties under reverse charge (18%) and can usually claim it back as input credit.

- Permanent establishment risk: if your staff run the Indian business day to day, India may tax a share of your profits directly. Keep roles clear in the agreement.

## Checking your Indian partner

A franchisee or licensee in India carries your brand. Before signing, check:

- Financial strength: filed accounts, borrowings and charges on assets; can they fund the store rollout they promise?

- Promoters: background, other businesses, litigation and regulatory history.

- Track record: other brands they run, and how those relationships ended.

- Related parties: property, supply and service deals with the promoter group that can drain margins or royalties.

- Real estate: lease terms and title for the planned locations.

See partner due diligence in India and how to verify an Indian company.

## Protect the brand first

- Register your trademarks in India before talking to partners; India is part of the Madrid Protocol.

- Put audit rights, sales reporting and royalty verification in the agreement.

- Agree exit terms: what happens to stores, stock and the brand if the relationship ends.

Related: appointing a distributor in India, joint ventures, taking profits out of India.

## Sources

- DPIIT (Consolidated FDI Policy, retail trading)
- RBI: Master Direction, Foreign Investment in India
- WIPO: Madrid System members (India)

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreign brand open its own stores in India?
Yes. Single-brand retail trading allows up to 100% FDI under the automatic route. Above 51% foreign ownership, at least 30% of the value of goods bought must be sourced from India, averaged over the first five years and then annually.

Do foreign franchisors need RBI approval to receive royalties from India?
No. Royalty and franchise fees are current-account payments that do not need RBI approval; the Indian partner pays through its bank after deducting withholding tax.

What is the withholding tax on royalties paid by an Indian company to a foreign brand owner?
20% plus surcharge and cess under Indian law, or the lower rate in the tax treaty with the brand owner's country if it provides a tax residency certificate and the required self-declaration.

Franchise or own stores in India: which is better?
Franchising needs no investment and gets you in faster, but your brand depends on the partner. Own stores give control but need capital and the 30% local sourcing rule above 51% FDI. Many brands start with a master franchise or JV and buy out later.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Sourcing · EU rules · Definitive since 1 January 2026

# CBAM and Indian suppliers: what EU importers need from India

The EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) moved from reporting to paying on 1 January 2026. Importers of Indian steel, aluminium, cement and fertilisers will buy certificates for the emissions embedded in 2026 imports from February 2027. Whether you pay on your supplier’s real emissions or on the EU’s higher default values depends on the data you get from India now.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Get supplier data checked
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Definitive CBAM since 1 Jan 2026; authorised declarant above 50 tonnes a year.
- Certificates from 1 Feb 2027; first declaration for 2026 imports by 30 Sep 2027.
- Get verified, installation-level emissions data from each Indian producer, or pay default values.

Quick answer: above 50 tonnes a year of CBAM goods you must be an authorised CBAM declarant. For 2026 imports you file the first annual declaration and surrender certificates by 30 September 2027; certificate sales start on 1 February 2027. Get installation-level, verified emissions data from each Indian producer, or default values (usually more expensive) apply.

## Key dates

Date | What happens | 

1 January 2026 | Definitive regime starts; authorised-declarant status needed above the 50-tonne annual threshold | 

1 February 2027 | CBAM certificate sales begin, covering 2026 imports | 

30 September 2027 | First annual CBAM declaration for 2026 imports, and surrender of certificates | 

Covered goods: iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity, including many downstream steel and aluminium products such as screws, bolts and structures. The 50-tonne threshold is cumulative net mass per importer per year (it does not apply to hydrogen and electricity).

## Why Indian supply matters

- India is a major exporter of steel and aluminium to the EU, and much Indian production is carbon-intensive (coal-based blast furnaces and coal-based DRI).

- There is no CBAM exemption for India under the India–EU trade deal; see the India–EU FTA guide.

- Producers vary widely: an electric-arc furnace using scrap has a very different footprint from an integrated plant. Your CBAM cost per tonne will differ by supplier.

## What you need from each Indian producer

- Installation details: which plant made your goods, and its production route.

- Embedded emissions (direct, and indirect where relevant) per tonne of each product, including precursors such as the steel used to make your parts.

- Verification by an accredited verifier, with access to the installation.

- Consistency: the data should match the products, quantities and plants on your invoices and shipping documents.

## Checking an Indian supplier’s data

Check | Why | 

Is the named plant the one that actually produced your goods? | Traders and job-workers can blur the origin | 

Does the reported route (EAF, BF-BOF, DRI) match the plant? | Route drives emissions; claims should match capacity and inputs | 

Who supplies precursors, and are their emissions included? | Missing precursor data understates emissions | 

Will the producer allow a verifier on site? | Unverified data may not be accepted | 

Company checks: ownership, finances, litigation | A supplier who can’t support you through 2027 is a cost risk | 

## What to do now

- Confirm your authorised-declarant status and your 2026 volumes by product and supplier.

- Send each Indian producer a data request now; prioritise the largest volumes and the most emissions-intensive routes.

- Check a sample on the ground: plant, route, records and precursors.

- Build CBAM cost into supplier pricing and contracts for 2027 onwards: data delivery, verification access and who bears default-value penalties.

Related: EUDR and Indian suppliers, sourcing from India, vendor due diligence.

## Sources

- DEHSt (German Emissions Trading Authority): CBAM definitive regime from 2026
- Kopik: CBAM 2026 deadlines, declarations and certificate dates
- CBAMfix: CBAM deadlines 2026 and 2027
- Carboneer: CBAM enters the definitive period

## Frequently asked questions
Does CBAM apply to steel imported from India?
Yes. Iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity from India are covered, with no exemption under the India–EU trade deal. Since 1 January 2026, importers above 50 tonnes a year must be authorised CBAM declarants.

When do EU importers pay CBAM on 2026 imports?
Certificate sales start on 1 February 2027, and the first annual declaration for 2026 imports, with surrender of certificates, is due by 30 September 2027.

What emissions data do EU importers need from Indian suppliers?
Installation-level embedded emissions per tonne of each product, including precursors, ideally verified by an accredited verifier. Without it, EU default values apply, which are usually higher.

What is the CBAM 50-tonne threshold?
Importers bringing in 50 tonnes or less of CBAM goods in a year (by cumulative net mass, excluding hydrogen and electricity) are outside the obligations. Above that, authorised-declarant status is needed.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Sourcing · EU rules · Applies 30 December 2026

# EUDR and Indian suppliers: what EU buyers need before 30 December

The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) applies to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026, after two postponements; the Commission’s May 2026 review ruled out another. If you place Indian coffee, rubber, wood products or other covered goods on the EU market, you need to trace them back to the plot of land and prove they were produced legally. With smallholder-heavy supply chains, that is the hard part in India.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Get suppliers checked
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Applies 30 December 2026 (large/medium); 30 June 2027 (micro/small, non-timber).
- Need plot geolocation, deforestation-free since 31 Dec 2020, legality under Indian law.
- Smallholder coffee and rubber chains in India need on-the-ground verification.

Quick answer: for each shipment you need the geolocation of every plot where the commodity was produced, evidence that it is deforestation-free since 31 December 2020 and legally produced under Indian law, a risk assessment, and a due diligence statement filed in the EU system. Large and medium operators: from 30 December 2026. Micro and small operators (outside timber): from 30 June 2027.

## What is covered

Commodity | Indian supply chains affected | 

Coffee | Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu estates and smallholders; green and roasted coffee | 

Rubber | Natural rubber (mainly Kerala) and listed rubber products such as tyres | 

Wood | Furniture, handicrafts, paper and packaging, plywood | 

Soya, cocoa, oil palm | Soya meal, cocoa products, palm-based derivatives | 

Cattle | Listed cattle products; check the current scope for leather, which the Commission has proposed changing | 

## What you need from Indian suppliers

- Geolocation: GPS points (or polygons for plots over 4 hectares) for every plot that produced the goods in the shipment.

- Deforestation-free evidence: no deforestation (or forest degradation, for wood) on those plots after 31 December 2020.

- Legality: production complied with Indian law: land-use rights, environmental rules, labour and human rights, tax, and forest rules for wood.

- Traceability through aggregators, processors and exporters, without mixing compliant and unknown material.

- Your own risk assessment and mitigation, then the due diligence statement before placing goods on the market or exporting.

## Where Indian supply chains struggle

- Smallholders: coffee and rubber come from very large numbers of small farms, often through local traders, so plot data is scattered.

- Land records: plot boundaries and ownership need to be matched to state land records; informal tenancy is common.

- Aggregation and mixing: curing works, rubber dealers and processors combine lots from many sources.

- Documentation quality: exporters may offer certificates or declarations that do not cover every plot in your shipment.

## How to check an Indian supplier

Check | What good looks like | 

Supplier mapping | A list of farms or estates, aggregators and processors behind each shipment | 

Geolocation data | Plot coordinates you can test against satellite deforestation layers | 

Land and legality evidence | Land records, permits and labour compliance for a sample of plots, verified on the ground | 

Segregation | Physical separation of EUDR-compliant lots through processing and shipping | 

Company checks | Exporter’s registration, ownership, financial health and litigation; see how to verify an Indian company | 

Desk reviews miss the gaps that matter: plots that don’t exist, coordinates copied across farms, or a trader who can’t say where 30% of the volume came from. Sample site visits are what give a buyer confidence.

## What to do before 30 December

- List the covered products you import from India and their suppliers.

- Ask each supplier for plot-level data and a traceability description now; prioritise the largest volumes.

- Verify a sample on the ground in India.

- Update contracts: data delivery, segregation, audit rights, and what happens if goods fail.

Related: UFLPA and traceability from Indian suppliers, sourcing from India, India–EU FTA.

## Sources

- European Commission: EU Deforestation Regulation
- EY: EUDR application postponed to 30 December 2026
- Law firm briefing (hlc.com): Commission publishes simplification package ahead of December 2026
- Mayer Brown: EUDR, what lies ahead in 2026
Importing steel or aluminium? CBAM and Indian suppliers: the data you need.

## Frequently asked questions
When does the EUDR apply?
From 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators and traders, and from 30 June 2027 for micro and small enterprises outside the timber sector. The Commission's May 2026 review ruled out another delay.

Does the EUDR apply to coffee and rubber from India?
Yes. Coffee and rubber are covered commodities, as are wood, soya, cocoa, oil palm and cattle, and listed products made from them. EU operators need plot-level geolocation and proof of deforestation-free, legal production.

What does an EU buyer need from an Indian supplier under the EUDR?
Geolocation of every plot that produced the goods, evidence of no deforestation after 31 December 2020, evidence of legal production under Indian law, and traceability through aggregators and processors so compliant goods are not mixed with unknown sources.

How can EU buyers verify Indian suppliers for the EUDR?
Map the supply chain behind each shipment, test plot coordinates against satellite data, check land and legality documents for a sample of plots on the ground, confirm segregation through processing, and run standard company checks on the exporter.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Compliance · UK companies in India · 2026

# UK failure to prevent fraud: what it means for your India operations

Since 1 September 2025, a large organisation can be prosecuted in the UK if someone acting for it commits fraud intended to benefit it, unless it had reasonable procedures to prevent fraud. For UK groups, many of those “associated persons” sit in India: sales agents, distributors, the Indian subsidiary, an offshore centre, outsourced call-centre staff. Here is how to cover them.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Review your India risk
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Large UK organisations are liable for fraud by associated persons, including those in India.
- Indian agents, subsidiaries, GCCs, call centres and service providers can all be associated persons.
- Defence: reasonable procedures that actually reach India: risk assessment, due diligence, contracts, monitoring.

Quick answer: if your organisation is large (two of: more than 250 employees, more than £36 million turnover, more than £18 million assets), fraud by your Indian agents, subsidiary, offshore centre or service providers that is meant to benefit you can make you liable. Your defence is reasonable fraud prevention procedures, which need to reach India: a risk assessment, due diligence on Indian partners, contract clauses, training and monitoring.

## The offence in brief

Point | Rule | 

Law | Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023; in force 1 September 2025 | 

Who is caught | Large organisations, including groups measured together and overseas organisations with a UK connection | 

Associated persons | Employees, agents, subsidiaries, and anyone providing services for or on behalf of the organisation | 

What triggers it | A listed fraud offence (for example false representation, false accounting, cheating the public revenue) intended to benefit the organisation or its clients | 

Defence | Reasonable fraud prevention procedures, as described in Home Office guidance | 

Penalty | Unlimited fine | 

## Where India comes in

- Sales agents and distributors who misstate products, fake documents or misrepresent terms to win business for you.

- Your Indian subsidiary or GCC producing false reports, inflated figures or misleading information to customers.

- Outsourced call centres and BPOs mis-selling or misleading UK customers on your behalf.

- Suppliers providing services for you who falsify certificates or test results that you pass on to customers.

The UK Bribery Act already required similar thinking for bribery. Many groups can extend the same programme, but fraud risks (mis-selling, false accounting, document fraud) are different from bribery risks and need their own assessment.

## Making “reasonable procedures” reach India

- Top-level commitment: the board owns fraud prevention, including overseas operations.

- Risk assessment: list your Indian associated persons and how each could commit fraud that benefits you.

- Proportionate procedures: approval controls, segregation of duties and reporting lines in the Indian entity.

- Due diligence: background checks on Indian agents, distributors and service providers before appointment and periodically. See partner due diligence in India.

- Communication and training: for staff and partners in India, in practical terms.

- Monitoring and review: audits of the Indian entity and key partners, whistleblowing channels people trust, and follow-up on red flags.

## Contract clauses for Indian partners

- Warranties against fraud and false documents; compliance with your code of conduct.

- Audit and information rights, including over sub-contractors.

- Duty to report suspected fraud; cooperation with investigations.

- Termination for breach without penalty.

## India red flags to look for

- Agents who resist due diligence or ask for payment to third parties.

- Commission levels well above the market.

- Indian entity results that consistently beat targets with weak documentation.

- Complaints from customers about what your Indian call centre told them.

Related: anti-bribery law for foreign companies in India, signs of fraud in an Indian subsidiary, vendor due diligence in India.

## Sources

- CMS: failure to prevent fraud, reasonable procedures guidance published
- WilmerHale: UK failure to prevent fraud offence to come into force
- Sidley: the new UK corporate offence of failure to prevent fraud
- K&L Gates: UK Fraud Strategy Framework 2026 to 2029

## Frequently asked questions
Does the UK failure to prevent fraud offence apply to Indian subsidiaries and agents?
It can. Associated persons include employees, agents, subsidiaries and anyone providing services for or on behalf of a large organisation. If they commit a listed fraud intended to benefit the organisation or its clients, the organisation can be liable unless it had reasonable fraud prevention procedures.

Which organisations are caught by the failure to prevent fraud offence?
Large organisations meeting two of three tests: more than 250 employees, more than £36 million turnover and more than £18 million total assets, measured across the group. It has applied since 1 September 2025.

What are reasonable fraud prevention procedures for India operations?
A risk assessment of Indian associated persons, proportionate controls in the Indian entity, due diligence on Indian agents, distributors and service providers, training, contract clauses with audit rights, and monitoring including whistleblowing channels.

What is the penalty for failure to prevent fraud?
An unlimited fine for the organisation, plus the reputational and contractual consequences.

Deals · Financial services · 2026

# Investing in an Indian bank or NBFC: limits, approvals and diligence

Foreign capital is pouring into Indian finance: Blackstone agreed in November 2026 to take more than 15% of IIFL Finance, Fairfax raised its stake in IIFL Capital to 38%, and the government chose Fairfax to buy 60.7% of IDBI Bank for about US$5.5 billion. Lenders are the most regulated businesses in India to invest in. Here is what applies before you sign.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Plan the investment
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Private banks: FDI cap 74%; RBI approval to reach 5%.
- NBFCs: 100% automatic, but RBI approval for control, 26%+ or 30%+ board change.
- Diligence: asset quality, provisioning, funding, RBI findings, related-party loans.

Quick answer: foreign investment in private banks is capped at 74% (up to 49% automatic, above that with government approval), and anyone reaching 5% of a bank needs RBI’s prior approval. NBFCs can be 100% foreign-owned under the automatic route, but a change in control, 26% or more of the shares, or more than 30% of the directors needs RBI’s prior approval.

## The rules side by side

| Private sector bank | NBFC (RBI-regulated) | 

FDI limit | 74%: up to 49% automatic, 49% to 74% government route | 100% automatic | 

RBI approval | Prior approval to reach a “major shareholding” of 5% or more (2023 Master Direction); fresh approval to go back above 5% after falling below | Prior approval for a change in control, acquisition of 26% or more, or a change of more than 30% of directors (excluding independent directors) | 

Holding caps | Limits on individual and non-promoter holdings; promoters capped at 26% after 15 years. RBI can allow more case by case | No general cap; fit-and-proper test for the acquirer | 

Listed target | SEBI takeover code: acquiring 25% or more, or control, triggers an open offer | 

Competition | CCI approval if asset, turnover or deal-value thresholds are crossed | 

## How the approvals fit together

- Structure the deal (primary issue, secondary purchase or both) and check the sector cap, including indirect foreign holding.

- Apply to RBI through the target with the acquirer’s fit-and-proper information, source of funds and business plan. Expect detailed questions on the ultimate owners.

- File with CCI where thresholds are crossed; prepare the open offer if the target is listed.

- Close, then report the foreign investment (FC-GPR for a fresh issue, FC-TRS for a purchase).

Investors with any Chinese or other land-border-country owners face an extra layer: see Press Note 2 (2026).

## Due diligence on an Indian lender

- Asset quality: gross and net NPAs, special-mention accounts, restructured and written-off loans, and how the book behaves when you re-age it yourself.

- Provisioning and capital: whether provisions cover the real stress; capital adequacy before and after your money.

- Funding and liquidity: borrowing concentration, asset-liability mismatches, reliance on short-term money.

- Regulatory history: RBI inspection findings and penalties, compliance with directions on digital lending, co-lending, KYC and outsourcing.

- Related parties: loans to promoters’ group companies, evergreening through connected borrowers.

- Collections and conduct: recovery agents, customer complaints, mis-selling risk.

- Technology and data: loan management systems, data localisation and cyber-security audits.

Read red flags in Indian company financial statements and our due diligence service.

## Sources

- Business Standard: RBI prior approval needed for over 5% stake in banks
- Chambers: new RBI directions on bank acquisitions in India
- Reuters via TradingView: Blackstone to buy over 15% stake in IIFL Finance
- CNBC: India to sell IDBI Bank stake to Fairfax for $5.5 billion
- Business Standard: Fairfax India raises stake in IIFL Capital to 38%

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreign company own an Indian bank?
Foreign investment in a private sector bank is allowed up to 74%: up to 49% under the automatic route and up to 74% with government approval. Anyone reaching 5% or more of a bank also needs the RBI's prior approval, and RBI caps on individual holdings apply.

Can an NBFC in India be 100% foreign-owned?
Yes. NBFCs regulated by the RBI can take 100% foreign investment under the automatic route, subject to minimum capitalisation norms. A change in control, acquisition of 26% or more, or a change of more than 30% of directors needs the RBI's prior approval.

When is RBI approval needed to buy shares in an Indian bank?
Before reaching a major shareholding of 5% or more of the bank's paid-up capital or voting rights, under RBI's 2023 Master Direction on acquisition and holding of shares or voting rights in banking companies.

What should due diligence on an Indian NBFC cover?
Asset quality (NPAs, restructured and written-off loans), provisioning and capital, funding and liquidity, RBI inspection findings and penalties, compliance with digital lending, co-lending and KYC rules, related-party lending and collection practices.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Sourcing · Aerospace and defence · 2026

# Sourcing aerospace and defence parts from India: what to verify first

Global engine and airframe makers are buying more from India. GE Aerospace has said it plans to nearly double its Indian supplier spend, to about US$400 million a year by 2030, with partners such as Tata Advanced Systems, Mahindra Aerostructures and Godrej making engine parts. For a buyer, the hard part is not finding suppliers but proving that a supplier’s certificates, licences and ownership are what they say.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Get a supplier checked
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Verify AS9100 (IAQG OASIS) and Nadcap (eAuditNet) against the actual site.
- Check defence and export licences, ownership and land-border links.
- Screen agents and public-sector dealings for bribery risk.

Quick answer: before awarding an aerospace or defence contract to an Indian supplier, verify its AS9100 certificate in the IAQG OASIS database and any Nadcap approvals for special processes, check licences (industrial licence for defence items, export licences for dual-use goods), map its owners (including any land-border-country links), test its financial health, and screen for bribery and agent risk.

## Why buyers are looking at India

- Large aerospace groups already source engine and airframe parts from Indian suppliers, and are expanding.

- Defence: foreign investment of up to 74% is allowed under the automatic route for companies seeking new industrial licences, so foreign OEMs can also set up or buy into Indian manufacturers. The government can review any defence investment on national-security grounds.

- Domestic programmes and offset or indigenisation requirements push foreign primes to build Indian supply chains.

## The checks that matter

Area | What to verify | How | 

Quality system | AS9100 certificate: scope, sites covered, expiry | IAQG OASIS database; match the legal entity and address | 

Special processes | Nadcap for heat treatment, NDT, coatings, welding, chemical processing | PRI eAuditNet; check which processes and which site | 

Customer approvals | Approved-supplier status with the OEMs it claims | Ask for supplier codes and approval letters; confirm with the OEM where possible | 

Defence licence | Industrial licence for defence items, where the products need one | Licence copy, product scope and conditions | 

Civil aviation | DGCA approvals where the supplier produces parts for aircraft certified in India | Approval certificates and scope | 

Export controls | SCOMET licences for dual-use exports from India; ability to handle ITAR or EAR-controlled data you send | Export licence history, controlled-data procedures, screening of staff and sub-suppliers | 

Ownership | Ultimate owners, related parties, any land-border-country ownership | MCA records, shareholding filings; see Press Note 2 (2026) | 

Financial health | Can it fund long qualification cycles and tooling? | Filed accounts, credit rating, bank borrowings, charges on assets | 

Integrity | Use of agents, public-sector customers, past investigations | Litigation and media searches, agent agreements, anti-bribery policy | 

## Bribery and agent risk

Defence and aerospace work in India often involves public-sector customers and intermediaries. If you are covered by the US FCPA, the UK Bribery Act or similar laws, a supplier’s payments to agents can become your problem. Ask who the supplier pays to win government work, review those contracts, and add audit and termination rights. See anti-bribery law for foreign companies in India.

## Red flags

- Certificate held by a group company or a different site from the one making your parts.

- Expired or suspended certificates, or scope that does not cover your process.

- Heavy reliance on one customer, or sudden growth without matching capital spending.

- Unexplained related-party transactions or frequent changes in directors.

- Reluctance to let you audit sub-suppliers who do special processes.

## A practical sequence

- Desk checks: certificates, MCA records, accounts, litigation and media.

- Site visit and process audit by someone who knows aerospace manufacturing.

- Ownership and integrity review, including agents.

- Contract with quality, export-control, anti-bribery and audit clauses.

- Ongoing monitoring: certificate expiry, financial filings, changes in owners.

Related: vendor due diligence in India, contract manufacturing checklist, sourcing from India.

## Sources

- GE Aerospace: plans to nearly double supplier spend in India
- IBEF: GE Aerospace to boost India supply-chain spending to US$400 million by 2030
- Legal500: up to 74% FDI under the automatic route in defence

## Frequently asked questions
How do I verify an Indian aerospace supplier's AS9100 certificate?
Search the IAQG OASIS database for the supplier, and check that the certified legal entity, site address and scope match the facility that will make your parts, and that the certificate is current.

Can foreign companies invest in Indian defence manufacturers?
Yes. Foreign investment of up to 74% is permitted under the automatic route for companies seeking new industrial licences; higher stakes need government approval, and the government can review defence investments on national-security grounds.

What export licences apply to aerospace parts from India?
Dual-use items on India's SCOMET list need an export licence from DGFT. Separately, if you share US-controlled technical data, the supplier must be able to comply with ITAR or EAR requirements you flow down.

What are red flags when sourcing aerospace parts from India?
Certificates held by a different entity or site, expired or narrow certificate scope, dependence on one customer, unexplained related-party dealings, frequent director changes and refusal to allow audits of special-process sub-suppliers.

FDI · Land-border investors · 2026

# Press Note 2 (2026): investing in India with land-border-country owners

Since 2020, any investment into India with an investor or beneficial owner in a country that shares a land border with India (most often China) has needed government approval. Press Note 2 (2026 Series) relaxed this for small, non-controlling stakes. For global funds with Chinese LPs, Asian holding companies and JV partners, the question is now: which side of the 10% line are you on?

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Check your ownership chain
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Up to 10% non-controlling land-border beneficial ownership: automatic route, where the sector allows.
- Above 10% or any control: government approval still needed.
- Map the investor's ownership to individuals and keep the evidence for the bank.

Quick answer: if the land-border-country beneficial ownership in the investor is 10% or less and non-controlling, the investment can go through the automatic route where the sector allows it, with extra reporting. More than 10%, or any control, still needs government approval.

## What changed

| Press Note 3 (2020) | Press Note 2 (2026) | 

Who is caught | Investor, or beneficial owner of the investment, in a land-border country | Same countries; beneficial ownership measured against a 10% threshold | 

Small, passive LBC ownership | Government approval needed, however small | Automatic route for non-controlling beneficial ownership up to 10%, subject to sector rules | 

Above 10% or control | Government approval | Government approval (still) | 

Reporting | Through the approval process | Investments with any LBC ownership are reported even when no approval is needed | 

The Press Note was issued on 15 March 2026; commentators report the matching FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules amendment as effective from 1 May 2026. Some reports also mention a 60-day fast-track for approvals in certain manufacturing sectors. Check the current DPIIT and FEMA text for your case.

The land-border countries are China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Afghanistan. Investors from Pakistan and Bangladesh face separate restrictions as well.

## Who this affects in practice

- Global and Asian funds with Chinese or Hong Kong-based limited partners.

- Singapore, Hong Kong or Cayman holding companies whose shareholders trace back to China.

- Foreign JV partners and acquirers with a Chinese strategic shareholder somewhere up the chain.

- Indian startups raising from funds with any LBC money in them.

## How to apply the 10% test

- Map the ownership chain of the investor up to the individuals, including funds’ LPs where relevant.

- Measure beneficial ownership held by LBC citizens or entities, using the beneficial-owner thresholds of the anti-money-laundering (PML) rules that the Press Note follows.

- Check control: board seats, vetoes, affirmative votes or management rights for the LBC holder take the case out of the automatic route even below 10%.

- Check the sector: the automatic route is only available where the sector allows it, within the cap.

- Document it: the Indian company’s bank will ask for beneficial-ownership declarations when the investment is reported (FC-GPR or FC-TRS). Keep the ownership chart and evidence on file.

## If you get it wrong

- Taking LBC-linked money without a needed approval is a FEMA contravention. It can mean unwinding the investment, or compounding with RBI and a penalty. See FEMA compounding.

- Later investors and acquirers will check this in diligence. A gap can delay or reprice a deal.

Related: acquiring a company in India, joint ventures in India, India FDI updates 2026.

## Sources

- Saraf Partners: DPIIT issues Press Note No. 2 (2026 Series)
- INAAC Advisors: FDI Press Note 2 (2026), investors with land-border ownership
- Sansa Legal: Press Note 2 (2026), beneficial ownership tests
- PwC India: DPIIT amends FDI policy on investments from land-border countries

## Frequently asked questions
What is Press Note 2 of 2026?
A DPIIT amendment, issued on 15 March 2026, to the 2020 rule on investment from countries sharing a land border with India. Investors whose land-border-country beneficial ownership is non-controlling and up to 10% can use the automatic route where the sector allows it; larger or controlling stakes still need government approval.

Can a fund with Chinese investors invest in India without approval?
Under Press Note 2 (2026), yes if the Chinese or other land-border beneficial ownership in the investor is 10% or less and carries no control, and the sector is under the automatic route. The investment must still be reported, and the ownership chain documented.

Which countries are covered by India's land-border FDI rule?
China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Afghanistan.

What happens if an Indian company takes land-border money without approval?
It is a FEMA contravention. The company may have to unwind the investment or apply to RBI for compounding with a penalty, and the gap will surface in later due diligence.

Startups · Fundraising · 2026

# Early-stage VCs in India: who writes the first cheque

Most Indian startups raise their first institutional money from a seed fund or the early-stage arm of a larger VC, often alongside angels. Here are the main types of early-stage investors, well-known names in each, what they check before investing, and the filings that follow.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Get investor-ready
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Seed funds, generalist VCs with seed programmes, sector funds and angel networks.
- Standard instrument: CCPS, with a registered valuer's report.
- Foreign VC money: FEMA fair value + FC-GPR within 30 days.

Quick answer: early-stage money in India comes from four places: dedicated seed funds (for example Blume Ventures, 3one4 Capital, Antler India, Better Capital, Titan Capital, India Quotient), generalist VCs with seed programmes (Peak XV Partners and its Surge programme, Accel, Elevation Capital, Lightspeed, Z47, Nexus), sector specialists (Fireside Ventures for consumer brands, Omnivore for agri and food, Speciale Invest for deep tech) and angel networks and funds. Check each firm’s current focus and stage on its website before you pitch.

## Types of early-stage investors

Type | Well-known examples | Typical stage | 

Seed and early-stage funds | Blume Ventures, 3one4 Capital, Kalaari Capital, Chiratae Ventures, Stellaris Venture Partners, India Quotient, Prime Venture Partners, Kae Capital, Arkam Ventures, Java Capital | Pre-seed to Series A | 

Generalist VCs with seed programmes | Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia India and SEA; Surge), Accel, Elevation Capital, Lightspeed, Z47 (formerly Matrix Partners India), Nexus Venture Partners | Seed to growth | 

Accelerators and pre-seed | Antler India, Y Combinator (global, accepts Indian founders), Surge | Idea to seed | 

Founder-led and micro funds | Better Capital, Titan Capital, All In Capital, First Cheque | Pre-seed and seed | 

Sector funds | Fireside Ventures (consumer), Omnivore (agri and food), Speciale Invest (deep tech), WEH Ventures | Seed to Series A | 

Angel networks and angel funds | Indian Angel Network, Inflection Point Ventures, LetsVenture-led syndicates; see angel investors in India | Pre-seed and seed | 

Names and focus change: funds raise new vehicles, rebrand and shift stage. Use this as a starting map, not an endorsement.

## What early-stage VCs check

- Founders: background, why this team, and how much each founder owns and has committed.

- Market and traction: size of the problem, early revenue or usage, retention, and how fast it is growing.

- A clean company: incorporation documents, cap table, founder agreements and vesting, IP assigned to the company, ROC and tax filings up to date. Messy paperwork slows or kills deals at diligence.

- The numbers: a simple financial model, monthly burn and runway, and use of funds. See the runway calculator.

## How the money comes in

- Compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) are the standard instrument for VC rounds in India. Early cheques sometimes use compulsorily convertible debentures or iSAFE notes.

- Shares are issued by private placement or preferential allotment, with a registered valuer’s report.

- Foreign VCs (or Indian funds with foreign-controlled managers): the issue price cannot be below fair value under FEMA, and the company files Form FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment. See the startup funding guide.

- Some investors ask for a US holding company. Think hard before a flip; see Delaware flip and reverse flip.

## Before you pitch

- Clean cap table and founder agreements with vesting.

- Financial model and monthly MIS for at least the last 6 to 12 months.

- A data room: incorporation documents, contracts, IP assignments, statutory filings.

- Know your numbers: use the valuation and dilution calculators before you discuss terms.

- Read the term sheet clause by clause: term sheet guide.

## Sources

- Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia India and SEA)
- Z47 (formerly Matrix Partners India)
- RBI: Master Direction, Foreign Investment in India

## Frequently asked questions
Which VCs invest in early-stage startups in India?
Well-known early-stage investors include seed funds such as Blume Ventures, 3one4 Capital, Kalaari Capital, Chiratae Ventures, Stellaris Venture Partners and India Quotient; generalist VCs with seed programmes such as Peak XV Partners (Surge), Accel, Elevation Capital, Lightspeed, Z47 and Nexus; and accelerators such as Antler India. Check each firm's current focus before pitching.

What instrument do VCs use to invest in Indian startups?
Mostly compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS). Early rounds sometimes use compulsorily convertible debentures or iSAFE notes. Shares are issued with a registered valuer's report.

What filings are needed when a foreign VC invests in an Indian startup?
The issue price must be at least fair value under FEMA, certified by a CA, SEBI-registered merchant banker or practising cost accountant, and the company files Form FC-GPR with RBI through its bank within 30 days of allotment.

What do early-stage investors look for in India?
A strong founding team, a large problem with early traction, a clean company (cap table, founder vesting, IP assignment, compliance) and clear numbers: burn, runway and use of funds.

# NRI income tax calculator: what you owe, and what you get back

Enter your Indian income for FY 2026-27. The calculator applies the NRI rules (no ₹12 lakh rebate, special rates on capital gains), compares the new and old regimes, and shows whether the TDS already deducted means a refund.

Get your NRI return filed
hello@durgeshchavda.com

## How NRI tax is worked out

- Slab rates apply to salary, rent, interest and short-term gains on non-equity assets. New regime: nil up to ₹4 lakh, then 5% to 30% (30% above ₹24 lakh). Old regime: nil up to ₹2.5 lakh, 5%, 20%, then 30% above ₹10 lakh. NRIs don’t get the higher exemption for senior citizens.

- No rebate: the section 87A rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free for residents is not available to NRIs.

- Capital gains at special rates: 20% on short-term gains from listed shares and equity funds, 12.5% on long-term gains (above ₹1.25 lakh a year for listed equity). NRIs can’t set the basic exemption limit against these gains.

- Surcharge above ₹50 lakh of income (10%), ₹1 crore (15%), ₹2 crore (25%); capped at 15% on capital gains. Cess 4% on top.

- TDS on NRO interest is 30% plus cess, and property buyers deduct on the whole sale price, so many NRIs pay far more than their real tax and should file for a refund.

## Example

An NRI with ₹5 lakh of NRO interest suffers TDS of about ₹1.56 lakh (31.2%). Actual tax under the new regime: ₹5,200. Filing a return gets back about ₹1.5 lakh.

Full rules: NRI income tax slabs 2026-27 · NRI taxation guide · TDS when an NRI sells property.

## Frequently asked questions
How much tax does an NRI pay in India?
Under the new regime, NRIs pay nil on the first ₹4 lakh of slab income, then 5% to 30%, with no ₹12 lakh rebate. Capital gains are taxed at special rates: 20% on short-term gains from listed shares and 12.5% on long-term gains. Add surcharge on high incomes and 4% cess.

Do NRIs get the ₹12 lakh tax-free limit?
No. The section 87A rebate is only for residents, so an NRI with ₹12 lakh of Indian income pays tax on it (about ₹62,400 under the new regime, including cess).

Can an NRI choose the old tax regime?
Yes. NRIs can choose the old regime and claim deductions such as 80C and 80D. It helps mainly when deductions are large; the calculator compares both.

Why do NRIs get income tax refunds?
Banks deduct 30% plus cess on NRO interest and property buyers deduct TDS on the whole sale price, often far more than the real tax. Filing an Indian return gets the excess back.

IPO tax · Update 10 November 2026

# Tax on your Jio Platforms IPO profit: worked examples

Jio Platforms listed on 28 October 2026 at ₹1,358, a 21.36% premium to the ₹1,119 issue price. If you were allotted shares, here is what you owe on the profit, whether you sold on listing day, sold since, or are still holding.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·5 min read

Ask about your IPO tax
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Sold within 12 months: 20% STCG plus cess; 1 lot at listing price = ₹2,868 profit, ~₹597 tax.
- Not intraday income, and not covered by the ₹12 lakh rebate.
- Hold past 26 October 2027: 12.5% on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year.

Quick answer: sold within 12 months of allotment, your profit is a short-term capital gain taxed at 20% plus 4% cess. One lot (12 shares) sold at the ₹1,358 listing price makes ₹2,868 profit and about ₹597 tax. Hold for more than 12 months and the gain is long-term: 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year.

## The numbers

Detail | Jio Platforms IPO | 

Issue price (upper band) | ₹1,119 per share | 

Lot size | 12 shares (₹13,428 per lot) | 

Listing date and price | 28 October 2026, ₹1,358 on NSE and BSE | 

Listing gain | ₹239 per share, ₹2,868 per lot | 

## Worked examples (resident individual)

You | Profit | Tax | 

Sold 1 lot at ₹1,358 on listing day | ₹2,868 | 20% = ₹574, plus cess = ₹597 | 

Sold 14 lots (168 shares, the most a retail applicant could apply for within ₹2 lakh) at ₹1,358 | ₹40,152 | 20% = ₹8,030, plus cess = ₹8,352 | 

Sold 1 lot later, at ₹1,450, within 12 months | ₹3,972 | 20% plus cess = ₹826 | 

Holding 1 lot for more than 12 months, then selling | Any amount | Long-term: nil up to ₹1.25 lakh of total long-term equity gains in the year, 12.5% above that | 

Figures ignore brokerage (which reduces the gain) and surcharge (only relevant at high incomes). STT paid on the sale is not deductible.

## Rules that catch people out

- Listing-day selling is not “intraday” or speculative income. The shares sat in your demat account from allotment, so the profit is a capital gain.

- The 12 months run from allotment (26 October 2026), not from the date you applied.

- The ₹12 lakh rebate does not cover this tax. Short-term gains taxed at the special 20% rate are outside the new-regime rebate. If your total income is below the basic exemption limit, a resident can use the unused limit against the gain.

- Losses help. If you sold other shares at a loss in the same year, short-term losses can be set off against this gain.

- Report it in the capital gains schedule of your return for tax year 2026-27 (due 31 July 2027 for most individuals). Your broker’s capital gains statement has the figures. Pay advance tax by the next instalment date to avoid interest.

## If you are an NRI

- NRIs could apply through an NRE or NRO account linked to an NRI demat account. See can NRIs apply for IPOs in India.

- The broker deducts TDS on your gain at 20% (plus surcharge and cess) when you sell. NRIs cannot use the basic exemption limit against this gain.

- If your country of residence has a tax treaty with India, check whether it lets you claim relief or a credit there. Gains on shares are usually taxable in India.

- Money from an NRE-route sale can be repatriated freely; NRO proceeds fall within the US$1 million yearly limit with Forms 15CA/15CB.

Work out your own figures with the IPO tax calculator, or read the full guide on tax on IPO profit in India.

## Sources

- 5paisa: Jio Platforms IPO shares list at ₹1,358 on NSE, 21.36% premium
- HDFC Sky: Jio Platforms lists at ₹1,358 against ₹1,119 issue price
- Chittorgarh: Jio Platforms IPO details (price band, lot size, dates)

## Frequently asked questions
How much tax do I pay on Jio Platforms IPO listing gains?
If you sold within 12 months, 20% of the profit plus 4% cess. One lot of 12 shares sold at the ₹1,358 listing price against the ₹1,119 issue price makes ₹2,868 profit and about ₹597 tax.

Is selling Jio Platforms shares on listing day intraday income?
No. The shares were in your demat account from allotment, so the profit is a short-term capital gain taxed at 20%, not speculative business income.

Is Jio IPO profit covered by the ₹12 lakh rebate?
No. Tax on short-term gains at the special 20% rate is outside the new-regime rebate. A resident whose total income is below the basic exemption limit can use the unused limit against the gain.

When does Jio Platforms IPO profit become long-term?
After 12 months from allotment on 26 October 2026. Long-term gains on listed shares are tax-free up to ₹1.25 lakh a year in total and taxed at 12.5% above that.

Do NRIs pay tax on Jio Platforms IPO gains?
Yes. The broker deducts TDS at 20% plus surcharge and cess on short-term gains when an NRI sells, and the gain is reported in the NRI's Indian return.

Hiring in India · Labour Codes · 2026

# Employee benefits in India: what a foreign employer must offer

Hiring your first people in India, through a subsidiary, a branch or an employer of record? Indian law sets a floor of benefits that cannot be contracted out of, and the four Labour Codes that took effect on 21 November 2025 changed how several of them are calculated. Here is the floor, and what competitive employers add on top.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Set up India payroll
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Mandatory: PF (12%), ESI (lower earners), gratuity, statutory bonus, maternity leave, state leave.
- PF ceiling raised to ₹25,000 a month from 17 September 2026.
- Labour Codes: 50% wage rule, gratuity for fixed-term staff after a year, final dues in 2 working days.

Quick answer: the legal minimum is provident fund (12% employer contribution), ESI health insurance for lower earners, gratuity on leaving, a statutory bonus for lower earners, 26 weeks’ maternity leave, and paid leave under state law. To compete for talent, most foreign employers add group health insurance, term life cover and a performance bonus.

## Mandatory benefits

Benefit | Who it covers | Cost to the employer | 

Provident fund (EPF) | Mandatory for employees with wages up to ₹25,000 a month (raised from ₹15,000 on 17 September 2026); optional above that. Applies to establishments with 20 or more employees | 12% of wages (part goes to the pension scheme, up to ₹2,083 a month); the employee also contributes 12% | 

ESI (state health insurance) | Employees earning up to ₹21,000 a month, in covered establishments (generally 10 or more employees) | 3.25% of wages; employee 0.75% | 

Gratuity | Employees leaving after 5 years; fixed-term employees after 1 year (new under the Labour Codes) | 15 days’ wages for each completed year, capped at ₹20 lakh. Usually funded through an insurer | 

Statutory bonus | Employees earning up to ₹21,000 a month | 8.33% to 20% of wages a year, depending on profits | 

Maternity benefit | Women employees | 26 weeks’ paid leave for the first two children; crèche facility where 50 or more are employed | 

Paid leave and holidays | All employees | Set by the state Shops and Establishments Act and the Labour Codes; varies by state | 

Professional tax, Labour Welfare Fund | Depends on the state | Small state levies withheld from salary and/or paid by the employer | 

## What the Labour Codes changed

- The 50% wage rule. “Wages” means basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance. If excluded allowances are more than 50% of total pay, the excess is added back. Salary structures with a low basic and high allowances now cost more in PF and gratuity.

- Gratuity for fixed-term staff after one year of service, worked out pro rata.

- Full and final settlement within two working days of an employee leaving.

- Appointment letters for every employee, and a single registration and return regime as states notify their rules. Central rules came in May 2026; states are notifying theirs on a rolling basis, so check the state where your team sits.

- PF ceiling to ₹25,000 (notification S.O. 5109(E), 17 September 2026): more mid-level employees now fall under mandatory PF.

## What good employers add

- Group health insurance covering the employee’s spouse, children and often parents. Not mandatory, but expected by almost every professional hire.

- Term life and personal accident cover.

- Employer NPS contribution: tax-efficient for the employee, deductible up to 14% of salary under the new tax regime.

- Annual performance bonus and, for senior roles, ESOPs or RSUs in the foreign parent. See parent-company ESOPs for Indian employees.

- Meal cards, internet and home-office allowances, structured within the 50% rule.

## Which route you hire through

Route | Who runs payroll and benefits | Fits when | 

Employer of record (EOR) | The EOR, as the legal employer | A few hires, testing the market | 

Indian subsidiary | You, through your own PF, ESI and tax registrations | A growing team or a capability centre | 

Contractors | Nobody: contractors get no statutory benefits | Genuinely independent, project-based work only. Misclassification and permanent-establishment risk if they work like employees | 

See hiring in India without an entity and setting up a GCC in India.

## Checklist before the first hire

- Pick the route: EOR, subsidiary or branch.

- Register for PF, ESI (if applicable), professional tax and the state Shops and Establishments Act.

- Design the salary structure so “wages” are at least 50% of pay, and budget PF and gratuity on that base.

- Buy group health and gratuity insurance.

- Issue appointment letters and a leave policy that meets the state rules.

- Set up monthly payroll, TDS on salary and quarterly TDS returns.

## Sources

- PIB: EPFO raises wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000
- BDO India: implementation of the Labour Codes, effective 21 November 2025
- Upstox: EPFO wage ceiling hiked to Rs 25,000, Gazette notification
- Remunance: India Labour Codes 2026, employer impact and state rules

## Frequently asked questions
What benefits must a foreign company give employees in India?
Provident fund (12% employer contribution, mandatory up to ₹25,000 monthly wages), ESI for employees earning up to ₹21,000 a month, gratuity on leaving, a statutory bonus for lower earners, 26 weeks' maternity leave and paid leave under state law. Group health insurance is not mandatory but is expected.

Is PF mandatory for all employees in India?
PF is mandatory for employees whose wages are up to ₹25,000 a month (the ceiling was raised from ₹15,000 on 17 September 2026) in establishments with 20 or more employees. Above the ceiling, the employer and employee can agree to contribute.

Do fixed-term employees get gratuity in India?
Yes. Under the Code on Social Security, in force since 21 November 2025, fixed-term employees qualify for gratuity after one year of service, on a pro-rata basis. Other employees need five years.

Is health insurance mandatory for employees in India?
Only ESI, the state scheme, is mandatory, and only for employees earning up to ₹21,000 a month in covered establishments. Private group health insurance is optional but almost universal for professional roles.

What is the 50% wage rule under the Labour Codes?
Wages for PF, gratuity and other benefits mean basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance. If the allowances left out are more than 50% of total pay, the excess is added back to wages, which raises PF and gratuity costs.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Funds · Investors · 2026

# Category III AIF: minimum investment, tax and who can invest

Category III AIFs are India’s hedge-fund style vehicles: long-short, derivatives and other trading strategies, sold to investors who can put in at least ₹1 crore. The big difference from Category I and II is tax. A Category III fund pays tax itself, so your returns arrive after tax.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Talk through the AIF
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Minimum ticket ₹1 crore (₹25 lakh for the manager's employees and directors).
- No pass-through: the fund pays tax; trading income at the maximum marginal rate.
- Compare post-tax, post-fee returns with PMS and mutual funds before investing.

Quick answer: minimum investment is ₹1 crore per investor (₹25 lakh for employees and directors of the fund or its manager). The fund, not the investor, pays tax on its income: capital gains at capital-gains rates and trading (business) income at the maximum marginal rate. Distributions to investors are generally not taxed again.

## What a Category III AIF is

SEBI’s AIF Regulations put funds that use diverse or complex trading strategies, and may use leverage, including through listed or unlisted derivatives, in Category III. In practice that means long-short equity funds, absolute-return and hedge strategies, and some PIPE (private investment in public equity) funds.

Point | Category III rule | 

Minimum investment | ₹1 crore per investor per scheme; ₹25 lakh for employees and directors of the AIF or its manager | 

Minimum fund size | ₹20 crore per scheme | 

Structure | Usually a trust; open-ended or close-ended | 

Leverage | Allowed, within limits set by SEBI | 

Tax | At fund level (no pass-through) | 

TDS on payouts | The 10% TDS on investment-fund income applies to Category I and II funds, not Category III | 

Separately, SEBI’s 2025 amendments created “Accredited Investors only” schemes, and cut the minimum ticket for large value funds for accredited investors from ₹70 crore to ₹25 crore. These follow their own rules.

## How Category III is taxed

- No pass-through. The pass-through regime (section 224 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, earlier section 115UB) covers only Category I and II funds. A Category III trust is taxed through its trustee as a representative assessee.

- Capital gains on listed shares are taxed at the fund level at the normal rates: 20% for short-term gains and 12.5% for long-term gains, plus surcharge and cess.

- Trading and derivatives income is generally business income, taxed at the maximum marginal rate. With surcharge and cess, this is the most expensive part of a Category III fund’s tax bill.

- Determinate vs indeterminate trust: if investors’ shares are not determinate, the maximum marginal rate can apply to all income. A July 2025 Delhi High Court ruling held that a Category III trust is not indeterminate merely because investors are not named in the deed.

- In your hands: the fund has already paid tax, so distributions are generally not taxed again. Gains on redeeming or selling units need separate advice based on the fund’s structure; check the tax note in the placement memorandum.

## Category III vs PMS vs mutual funds

| Category III AIF | PMS | Equity mutual fund | 

Minimum | ₹1 crore | ₹50 lakh | No real minimum | 

Who pays tax | The fund | You, on every trade in your account | You, when you redeem | 

Derivatives and leverage | Allowed within SEBI limits | Limited | Limited (hedging) | 

Fees | Management fee plus performance fee, often above a hurdle | Management and/or performance fee | Expense ratio, capped by SEBI | 

Because a Category III fund pays tax at the fund level, your post-tax return depends heavily on the strategy’s mix of short-term gains and trading income. Ask the manager for post-tax returns, not just pre-tax.

## Who can invest

- Resident individuals, HUFs, companies, LLPs, trusts and family offices that meet the minimum and complete KYC.

- NRIs and OCIs can invest, on a repatriable or non-repatriable basis, subject to FEMA and the fund’s own terms. Because the fund pays Indian tax itself, NRIs may find it hard to use treaty benefits. A GIFT City fund can work better for money held abroad; see GIFT City fund vs SEBI AIF.

- Foreign investors can invest in AIF units under the automatic route, subject to SEBI’s eligibility requirements.

## Before you sign

- Check the fund’s SEBI registration in SEBI’s list of registered AIFs.

- Read the private placement memorandum: strategy, leverage, lock-in, exit loads and the tax note.

- Understand the fee stack: management fee, performance fee, hurdle and high-water mark.

- Ask for net-of-tax, net-of-fee returns for past periods.

- If you are an NRI, check how you will repatriate the money and whether your country of residence taxes the distribution again.

Related: how all AIF categories are taxed, AIF categories explained and setting up an AIF with SEBI.

## Sources

- EaseValue: Section 224, Income-tax Act 2025 (AIF pass-through)
- TDSMAN: TDS on income from investment fund, section 393 (old 194LBB)
- Legal500: SEBI amends the AIF Regulations (accredited investors, large value funds)
- SEBI board paper: proposals for accredited investors (Sep 2025)

## Frequently asked questions
What is the minimum investment in a Category III AIF?
₹1 crore per investor per scheme. Employees and directors of the AIF or its manager can invest from ₹25 lakh. Separate rules apply to accredited-investor-only schemes.

How is a Category III AIF taxed in India?
At the fund level. Category III AIFs do not get pass-through status, so the fund (usually a trust, through its trustee) pays tax: capital gains at capital-gains rates and trading or derivatives income at the maximum marginal rate. Distributions to investors are generally not taxed again.

Is there TDS on Category III AIF distributions?
The 10% TDS on income distributed by investment funds applies to Category I and II AIFs. Category III funds pay tax themselves, so that TDS provision does not apply to their distributions.

Can NRIs invest in Category III AIFs?
Yes, subject to FEMA, KYC and the fund's terms, on a repatriable or non-repatriable basis. Because the fund pays Indian tax itself, NRIs may not be able to use treaty benefits, so a GIFT City fund is sometimes a better fit.

Category III AIF or PMS: which is more tax-efficient?
It depends on the strategy. In a PMS every trade is taxed in your hands; in a Category III AIF the fund pays tax, with trading income at the maximum marginal rate. Compare post-tax, post-fee returns for your tax bracket.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.
