Hiring guide

# Hiring in India without an entity — and the tax risk nobody mentions

An employer of record solves payroll in a week. It doesn’t solve permanent establishment risk. Here’s how foreign companies hire in India safely as they grow.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Review your PE risk
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Employer of record arrangements are lawful in India.
- An EOR does not remove permanent-establishment risk if staff conclude contracts or work from premises at your disposal.
- Most companies move to a cost-plus subsidiary once the team grows past about ten people.

## Your three options

| Independent contractor | Employer of record (EOR) | Own subsidiary | 

Speed | Days | About 1–2 weeks | 1–2 months | 

Who employs them? | Nobody — a service contract | The EOR, which bills you | Your Indian company | 

Main risk | Misclassification; PE | PE; EOR seen as a sham if you control everything | Compliance workload | 

Usually fits | Genuinely independent specialists | First hires, market testing | Teams of roughly 10+, or long-term plans | 

## Is an employer of record legal in India?

Yes. India has no specific EOR law; it operates as a staffing arrangement, now within the four Labour Codes in force since 21 November 2025. The EOR runs payroll, provident fund, gratuity and statutory filings. What it can’t do is change how the tax authorities see your business.

## Permanent establishment: the real risk

- Dependent agent: India-based staff who habitually conclude contracts or negotiate prices for you can make you taxable in India. Keep signing and pricing authority outside India.

- Service PE: your people providing services in India beyond the treaty’s day threshold (for example 90 days under the India–US treaty) can create a PE.

- Fixed place: after the Supreme Court’s 2025 Hyatt ruling, premises at your disposal can be enough — you needn’t own or lease them.

- If a PE exists, India taxes the profit attributable to it — at foreign-company rates — and expects a return.

## How to stay safe

- Write clear role descriptions: support, engineering and research rather than sales closing.

- Keep contracts approved and signed abroad; avoid giving Indian staff authority to bind you.

- Track days of visiting staff against treaty thresholds.

- Move to a subsidiary with a cost-plus transfer-pricing model once the team is growing — the subsidiary then employs everyone and your PE risk falls sharply.

Need a review of your current set-up? See India tax for foreign companies, or set up properly with company setup in India.

## Sources

- HSF Kramer — India's Labour Codes implemented
- Treelife — permanent establishment risk in India
Related: paying Indian freelancers.
Hiring in India? Employee benefits a foreign employer must offer (2026).

## Frequently asked questions
Can a US company hire an employee in India without an entity?
Yes, through an employer of record or, for genuinely independent work, a contractor agreement. Both are lawful, but neither removes permanent establishment risk if Indian staff conclude contracts or the business operates from India.

Does using an EOR in India create a permanent establishment?
It can. An EOR handles employment, but if the workers habitually conclude contracts for you, provide services beyond treaty day limits or work from premises at your disposal, the tax authorities can treat you as having a PE.

When should a foreign company set up a subsidiary instead of using an EOR?
Usually once the team passes roughly ten people, includes sales or leadership roles, or is planned for the long term. A subsidiary with a cost-plus arrangement reduces PE risk and is often cheaper at scale.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Foreign parent guide

# Getting profits out of your Indian subsidiary

“How do we get profit out of our India subsidiary, and what is withheld?” is one of the most common questions from foreign CFOs. Here are the routes, the tax on each and the paperwork.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Plan your repatriation
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Dividends to a foreign company: 20% plus surcharge and cess, or the lower treaty rate with a TRC and Form 41.
- Service fees and royalties are deductible in India if at arm's length, but carry withholding.
- From 1 April 2026, buybacks are taxed as capital gains rather than dividends.

## The five routes

Route | Deductible for the Indian company? | Indian withholding (domestic) | 

Dividend | No — paid from post-tax profit | 20% plus surcharge and cess | 

Service / management fee | Yes, if at arm’s length and the service is real | Fees for technical services 20%; often nil or 10–15% under treaties | 

Royalty / licence fee | Yes, if at arm’s length | 20%; usually 10–15% under treaties | 

Interest on an intercompany loan | Yes, within interest-limitation rules | Depends on the loan; treaty rates commonly 10–15% | 

Buyback of shares | No | Capital gains in the parent’s hands from 1 April 2026 | 

## Dividend withholding by country

Parent company in | Treaty rate on dividends | 

United States | 15% with 10%+ of voting stock; otherwise 25% | 

United Kingdom | 10% (15% in some cases) | 

Singapore | 10% with 25%+ shareholding; otherwise 15% | 

UAE, Japan, Germany, Netherlands | 10% | 

No treaty / documents missing | 20% plus surcharge and cess | 

Treaty rates need a tax residency certificate, Form 41 and beneficial ownership of the dividend; anti-abuse rules (the MLI principal purpose test) can deny them. Check the treaty and its protocols for your case.

## The paperwork for every remittance

- From the parent: a tax residency certificate, Form 41 (formerly 10F) and, for fees and royalties, a no-PE declaration.

- From the Indian company: withholding under section 393(2), Form 145 online and a CA certificate in Form 146 where required, then the bank remittance.

- Board approvals for dividends; intercompany agreements and transfer-pricing support for fees, royalties and interest; ECB rules for loans.

## Choosing the mix

- Dividends are simple but come from post-tax profit; fees and royalties reduce Indian tax but invite transfer-pricing scrutiny.

- Withholding on fees can often be credited in the parent’s country — check your foreign tax credit position.

- Since April 2026, buybacks are taxed as capital gains (on the gain, not the whole payout) — worth modelling against a dividend.

We handle this for foreign parents — see Indian subsidiary compliance. US parent? Read the India–US tax treaty guide.

## Sources

- Income-tax Act, 2025 — section 207 (Taxsutra)
- Income Tax Department — Form 41 note
- Vinod Kothari — buyback taxation (Feb 2026)

## Frequently asked questions
How much tax is withheld on dividends paid to a foreign parent from India?
20% plus surcharge and cess under domestic law, reduced by the treaty — for example 15% for a US parent holding at least 10%, and 10% for UK, UAE, Japanese, German or Dutch parents — with a tax residency certificate and Form 41.

Can an Indian subsidiary pay management fees to its foreign parent?
Yes, if the services are real, priced at arm's length and documented. Withholding applies under section 393(2), often at a reduced treaty rate, and the fees are deductible for the Indian company.

How are share buybacks taxed in India from 2026?
From 1 April 2026 buyback proceeds are taxed as capital gains in the shareholder's hands — on the gain, after deducting cost — rather than as dividends. Promoters face additional tax.

Is there a limit on repatriating profits from India?
There is no cap on repatriating dividends from profits on which tax has been paid, provided company-law requirements are met and the remittance is documented with the bank.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Foreign SaaS guide

# GST for foreign SaaS selling into India

If you sell software, apps, streaming or online courses to Indian customers from abroad, Indian GST probably applies — and since 2023 it reaches more of your customers than you think.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Sort out your India GST
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Buying SaaS from abroad? the TDS side.
Key takeaways
- Foreign suppliers of online services to unregistered Indian customers register via GST REG-10 and charge 18% IGST.
- Since 1 October 2023 the OIDAR net covers any unregistered recipient, including unregistered businesses.
- Sales to GST-registered businesses are taxed under reverse charge; the equalisation levy has been abolished.

## Who is caught

- Online information and database access or retrieval (OIDAR) services: SaaS, cloud services, apps, digital content, online advertising, e-learning and similar.

- Since 1 October 2023 the old “essentially automated, minimal human intervention” test was removed, and a non-taxable online recipient now means any unregistered person in India — including unregistered businesses, not just consumers.

## Sales to consumers and unregistered businesses

- Register through the simplified Form GST REG-10 — no Indian entity needed.

- Charge 18% IGST and file GSTR-5A monthly by the 20th. No input tax credit.

- Appoint an Indian representative to pay tax if you have no presence in India.

## Sales to GST-registered businesses

The Indian customer pays GST under reverse charge. Collect and check their GSTIN — that’s your evidence the sale is B2B.

## What no longer applies

The 2% equalisation levy ended from 1 August 2024 and the 6% levy on online advertising from 1 April 2025. Income tax is separate: your treaty generally protects business profits unless you have a permanent establishment, though India also has significant economic presence rules.

## Practical steps

- Add a GSTIN field at checkout and validate it.

- Price in INR or show tax-inclusive prices for Indian consumers.

- Keep location evidence (billing address, IP, payment country) for each Indian sale.

## Sources

- ELP — OIDAR changes in Finance Act 2023
- India Briefing — abolition of the 2% equalisation levy
- BDO — 57th GST Council recommendations

## Frequently asked questions
Does a foreign SaaS company need GST registration in India?
Yes, if it supplies online services to Indian consumers or unregistered businesses. It registers through the simplified Form GST REG-10, charges 18% IGST and files GSTR-5A monthly. Sales to GST-registered businesses are taxed under reverse charge instead.

What is OIDAR in GST?
Online information and database access or retrieval services — services delivered over the internet such as SaaS, cloud services, digital content and online ads. Since October 2023 the definition no longer requires the service to be essentially automated.

Is the equalisation levy still applicable in India?
No. The 2% levy on e-commerce supplies ended from 1 August 2024 and the 6% levy on online advertising from 1 April 2025.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Foreign vendor guide

# Form 41, TRC and no-PE declaration — for foreign vendors paid by India

Indian customers withhold tax from many payments to foreign suppliers. These three documents are how you get your treaty rate instead of 20% — here’s what each one is and how to get it right.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 30 October 2026·6 min read

Get your vendor pack ready
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Paying or getting paid across borders? We file Form 41 for foreign vendors, TDS returns (Forms 140 and 144) and remittance forms (145/146) for Indian payers, and set up treaty rates correctly.Free 15-min callWhatsApp

Key takeaways
- Form 10F was renumbered Form 41 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026.
- A TRC, Form 41 and a no-PE declaration let an Indian payer apply your treaty rate instead of 20%.
- If tax was withheld at a lower treaty rate, a foreign company usually still has to file an Indian return.

## What is Form 41 in India?

Form 41 is the form a non-resident files on India’s income-tax portal to claim tax-treaty benefits. It replaced Form 10F from 1 April 2026 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, and gives the details a tax residency certificate may not contain — status, nationality, tax identification number, period and address. Indian payers ask for it, with a TRC and often a no-PE declaration, before applying a treaty withholding rate to payments abroad.

## Why your Indian customer is asking

Indian payers must withhold tax on many payments to non-residents under section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 — royalties and fees for technical services at 20% plus surcharge and cess under domestic law. To apply the lower rate in your country’s tax treaty (often 10–15%, or nil for ordinary business profits without a PE), they need evidence. If they get it wrong, the shortfall is theirs — so they ask.

## The documents

Document | What it is | Who issues it | 

Tax residency certificate (TRC) | Proof you are tax resident in your country for the year | Your home tax authority (e.g. IRS Form 6166 in the US, HMRC certificate in the UK) | 

Form 41 (formerly Form 10F) | Details the TRC doesn’t contain — status, nationality, tax ID, period, address | You, filed online on India’s income-tax portal | 

No-PE declaration | Your statement that you have no permanent establishment in India | You, on letterhead | 

Beneficial ownership declaration | That you are the beneficial owner of the income | You, on letterhead (often combined) | 

PAN | Indian tax ID: helps avoid higher withholding and is needed to file an Indian return. Not needed for Form 41, which can be filed without a PAN. | Indian income-tax department, on application | 

## Form 41: the new name for Form 10F (what the official FAQ says)

- From 1 April 2026, Form 10F (section 90(5) of the 1961 Act, Rule 21AB) became Form 41, a self-declaration under section 159(8) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 and Rule 75 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026. Indian payers may still say “10F”.

- Mandatory for a non-resident to claim treaty benefits. Without a valid Form 41 (with the TRC), the Indian payer must deduct tax at the full domestic rate, and an exemption claimed in a return is taxed at Indian rates.

- Online only, on the income-tax e-filing portal. No PAN needed: non-residents without a PAN register under the new “non-residents without PAN” category and verify by OTP sent to phone and email. With a PAN, verify by EVC (bank or demat account), net banking or a digital signature.

- Once per tax year (April to March). There is no fixed deadline, but it must be in place when treaty benefits are claimed, so file it before the first payment of the year.

- Attach: your tax residency certificate, valid for the relevant Indian financial year, and your tax identification number from your home country.

- Cannot be edited once submitted and acknowledged, so check every detail first. No proof of tax payment is needed, and Aadhaar is not required.

## Is the no-PE declaration true for you?

Only sign it if it’s accurate. Staff or contractors in India who conclude contracts for you, an office at your disposal, or long on-site projects can create a PE — see PE risk.

## Sample no-PE declaration (format)

Many Indian payers have their own template; if not, a declaration on the vendor’s letterhead usually covers these points. Illustrative only — adapt it to your facts and the relevant tax treaty, and check it with your adviser.

Declaration regarding permanent establishment

To: [Name of Indian payer], [address]
Date: [date]

We, [legal name of the foreign company], a company incorporated in [country] with its registered office at [address], declare for the period [from] to [to] that:

- We are a tax resident of [country] for this period, as shown in the enclosed Tax Residency Certificate issued by [authority].

- We do not have a permanent establishment in India within the meaning of Article 5 of the India–[country] Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement — including a fixed place of business, a dependent agent, or a service or installation PE.

- The income received from you under [invoice / agreement reference] is not effectively connected with any permanent establishment or fixed base in India.

- We are the beneficial owner of this income.

- We will inform you promptly if any of these facts change during the period.

Signed for and on behalf of [company] — [name], [designation]

Send it with the TRC and Form 41 (the information the TRC does not show). Only sign it if it is true — see is the no-PE declaration true for you?

## After you’re paid

- Your customer issues a certificate of the tax withheld; claim it as a foreign tax credit at home.

- If too much was withheld, a refund is claimed through an Indian return.

- If your only Indian income is royalties or technical fees and tax was withheld at the full domestic rate, you may not need to file. If a lower treaty rate was used, you usually do.

- Large recurring contracts: a lower-withholding certificate (Form 128) can help.

We can prepare this pack for you — India tax for foreign companies.

## Sources

- Income Tax Department — Form 41 FAQs
- Income Tax Department — Form 41 note

## Frequently asked questions
Is Form 41 the same as Form 10F?
Yes. Form 10F under the Income-tax Rules, 1962 became Form 41 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, from 1 April 2026.

What is Form 41 in India?
Form 41 is the Income-tax Rules 2026 replacement for Form 10F. A non-resident files it online to give the details a tax residency certificate may not contain, so that an Indian payer can apply treaty withholding rates.

What is a no PE declaration?
A declaration by a foreign company that it has no permanent establishment in India. Indian payers use it, with a TRC and Form 41, to apply treaty rates — for business profits, usually nil withholding.

Is a PAN mandatory for a foreign company receiving payments from India?
Not always. Without a PAN the payer may have to withhold at a higher rate unless prescribed details are provided, and filing an Indian return needs one. Form 41 itself can be filed without a PAN.

Can Form 41 be filed without a PAN?
Yes. According to the Income Tax Department's Form 41 FAQs, non-residents without a PAN can register on the e-filing portal under the category for non-residents without PAN and file Form 41 online, verifying by OTP.

Is Form 41 mandatory, and how often is it filed?
Yes, it is mandatory to claim treaty benefits. It is filed online once per tax year, with a tax residency certificate valid for that year and your home-country tax identification number.

Can I edit Form 41 after submitting it?
No. Once Form 41 is submitted and the acknowledgement is generated, it cannot be edited, so check the details before you submit.

How long is a TRC valid for Indian treaty purposes?
It covers the period stated on it — usually a tax year. Provide a TRC and Form 41 covering each period in which you receive payments.

What is the format of a no-PE declaration in India?
A short letter on the foreign company's letterhead stating its tax residence (with the TRC), that it has no permanent establishment in India under Article 5 of the relevant tax treaty, that the income is not connected with any PE in India, that it is the beneficial owner, and that it will report changes — signed by an authorised person.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

NRI taxation

# NRI taxation in India: the complete 2026 income-tax guide

Everything a non-resident Indian needs to know about Indian tax in one place — what’s taxed, at what rate, why TDS usually over-deducts, how treaties help, and how to get money back out.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·11 min read

Talk to a CA about NRI tax
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Hold anything abroad? FAST-DS 2026 closes on 31 December: a one-time chance to declare foreign accounts, RSUs and assets missed in your returns, from a flat ₹1 lakh. Check what you would pay or get it filed.

Quick reference: NRI income tax slab 2026-27 (no ₹12 lakh rebate, refund example).
Moved to Dubai? account-by-account checklist.
Quick answers

- Do NRIs have to pay tax in India? Yes — but only on Indian income: rent from Indian property, interest on NRO deposits, dividends, and capital gains on Indian shares, funds and property. Salary earned and paid abroad, and other foreign income, is not taxed in India.

- NRI tax slab 2026-27: the same slabs as residents (new regime: nil to ₹4 lakh, then 5% to 30%), but without the rebate that makes ₹12 lakh tax-free for residents.

- Interest on NRE and FCNR deposits is tax-free for NRIs; NRO interest is taxable.

- TDS: Indian payers deduct tax at source on most NRI income, often more than the final tax — file a return to get the excess back.

- Deemed resident: an Indian citizen with Indian income above ₹15 lakh who isn’t taxable in any other country can be treated as resident (RNOR) — check with the residential status calculator.

Work out your own tax: NRI income tax calculator, new vs old regime, with your refund against TDS.

## Who counts as an NRI for tax

For income tax, “NRI” means a non-resident under the day-count tests — it’s not about your passport or visa. You’re resident if you spend 182 days or more in India in the tax year, or 60 days plus 365 days in the previous four years (with relaxations for Indians working abroad or visiting, and a 120-day rule when Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh). Check yours with the residential status calculator or read residential status and RNOR.

## What India taxes

Income | Taxed in India for an NRI? | 

Salary for work done abroad, foreign rent, foreign interest | No | 

Rent from Indian property | Yes | 

NRO account interest | Yes (TDS at 30% plus surcharge and cess unless a treaty rate applies) | 

NRE and FCNR interest | No, while non-resident | 

Capital gains on Indian property, shares and mutual funds | Yes | 

Dividends from Indian companies | Yes | 

## NRI income tax slabs 2026-27

Taxable Indian income (new regime, default) | Rate for NRIs | 

Up to ₹4 lakh | Nil | 
₹4–8 lakh | 5% | 
₹8–12 lakh | 10% | 
₹12–16 lakh | 15% | 
₹16–20 lakh | 20% | 
₹20–24 lakh | 25% | 
Above ₹24 lakh | 30% | 

- No ₹12 lakh rebate for NRIs — the section 156 (old 87A) rebate is for residents only, so an NRI with ₹10 lakh of Indian income pays tax from ₹4 lakh.

- The old regime (nil to ₹2.5 lakh, 5%, 20%, 30%) is also available; NRIs don’t get the higher senior-citizen exemption limits.

- Plus surcharge above ₹50 lakh and 4% cess. Compare both regimes in the income tax calculator (choose “Non-resident”).

## Tax rates for NRIs

- Slab rates are the same as for residents. Under the new regime: nil up to ₹4 lakh, then 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% in ₹4 lakh steps, and 30% above ₹24 lakh.

- No section 87A rebate: the rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free for residents is not available to NRIs.

- Listed shares and equity funds: long-term gains (held over 12 months) at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year; short-term gains at 20%.

- Property: long-term gains (held over 24 months) at 12.5% without indexation; the 20%-with-indexation option for pre-July-2024 property is for residents only. Try the capital gains calculator.

- For NRIs, the unused basic exemption can’t be set off against these special-rate capital gains.

## TDS: why NRIs usually overpay

- Payments to NRIs carry TDS at full rates — on property sales, rent, NRO interest and capital gains on shares and funds.

- Because TDS ignores your slab and exemptions, it’s often more than your final tax — you recover the excess by filing a return.

- Before a big transaction, a lower-TDS certificate (Form 128) stops over-deduction in the first place.

- Selling property? Read TDS on sale of property by an NRI — including the no-TAN rule for buyers from 1 October 2026.

## Double tax relief (DTAA)

India’s tax treaties can cap Indian tax on interest, dividends and royalties below the domestic rate. Give the payer your tax residency certificate and Form 41 (formerly 10F). Treaty rates by country: US · UAE · Gulf · Europe · Canada · Australia.

## Bank accounts and repatriation

- NRE (foreign earnings, tax-free interest, freely repatriable) vs NRO (Indian income, taxable interest) — see NRE vs NRO vs FCNR.

- Up to USD 1 million per financial year can be repatriated from NRO balances and sale proceeds, with Forms 145 and 146 (formerly 15CA/15CB) — see repatriation.

## Filing your return

File if your Indian income exceeds the basic exemption limit — and whenever you want excess TDS back. Most NRIs use ITR-2. NRIs don’t report foreign assets. Details: NRI income tax return.

## Investing in India from abroad

NRIs can invest in Indian startups (with FEMA reporting), SEBI AIFs and GIFT City funds — and since 2026 individuals abroad can hold up to 10% of a listed Indian company through the portfolio route.

## NRI tax checklist

- Confirm your residential status for the year.

- Move resident accounts to NRO; keep foreign earnings in NRE/FCNR.

- Give banks your TRC and Form 41 to get treaty rates.

- Get a lower-TDS certificate before selling property or other large receipts.

- File your return to claim refunds; keep Form 146 certificates for repatriation.

Want it handled? See NRI taxation services.
Quick answers: India for NRIs and foreigners — questions answered.

## Recent ruling
In October 2026 the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Pune reportedly allowed a Singapore-based NRI’s refund claim under the India–Singapore treaty on mutual-fund gains, holding that missing the return deadline did not take away treaty relief (Business Today, 22 Oct 2026). Rulings turn on their facts — if you overpaid tax as an NRI, it is worth reviewing whether a refund is still available.

## Frequently asked questions
Do NRIs have to pay tax in India?
Yes, on income that arises or is received in India — such as rent, NRO interest, dividends and capital gains on Indian assets. Income earned and received outside India is not taxed in India for a non-resident.

What is the income tax slab for NRIs in India?
For tax year 2026-27 under the default new regime: nil up to ₹4 lakh, 5% to ₹8 lakh, 10% to ₹12 lakh, 15% to ₹16 lakh, 20% to ₹20 lakh, 25% to ₹24 lakh and 30% above, plus surcharge and cess. NRIs don't get the ₹12 lakh rebate available to residents.

Is NRE interest taxable in India?
No. Interest on NRE accounts and FCNR deposits is exempt for NRIs. Interest on NRO accounts is taxable and subject to TDS.

What are the income tax slabs for NRIs in 2026-27?
Under the default new regime: nil up to ₹4 lakh, 5% to ₹8 lakh, 10% to ₹12 lakh, 15% to ₹16 lakh, 20% to ₹20 lakh, 25% to ₹24 lakh and 30% above, plus surcharge and cess. NRIs don't get the rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free for residents.

How is an NRI taxed in India?
An NRI is taxed only on income earned or received in India — such as Indian rent, NRO interest, dividends and capital gains on Indian assets — at the same slab rates as residents but without the section 87A rebate. Foreign income isn't taxed in India.

Is the ₹12 lakh tax-free limit available to NRIs?
No. The section 87A rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free under the new regime applies only to resident individuals. NRIs pay tax from ₹4 lakh under the new regime slabs.

What is the capital gains tax for NRIs on shares?
On listed shares and equity mutual funds, long-term gains (held more than 12 months) are taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year and short-term gains at 20%, with TDS deducted at source for NRIs.

How can NRIs avoid double taxation?
By claiming the lower rate under India's tax treaty with their country of residence (with a tax residency certificate and Form 41) and claiming credit for Indian tax in their home country.

Do NRIs need to file an income tax return in India?
Yes, if Indian income exceeds the basic exemption limit — and it's usually worth filing anyway to claim refunds of excess TDS.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Cross-border tax guide

# India–US DTAA: treaty rates and how to actually claim them

Money moving between India and the US — dividends from your US company, fees from US clients, royalties to a US parent — is taxed in both countries unless you use the treaty correctly.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 17 October 2026·8 min read

Get treaty advice
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Quick answers
- Dividends: 15% if the US company holds at least 10% of voting stock, otherwise 25%.
- Interest: 10% on loans from banks and financial institutions, 15% otherwise.
- Royalties and fees for included services: generally 15% (10% for certain equipment royalties).
- To claim it: a US tax residency certificate (IRS Form 6166) and India’s Form 41.

## What the India–US DTAA does

The India–US Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (the 1989 Convention) decides which country may tax each type of cross-border income, caps the tax the source country can withhold, and requires the residence country to give credit for tax already paid. It is the reason a dividend from your Delaware company, or a service fee from a US client, doesn’t have to be taxed twice in full.

## Treaty rates at a glance

Maximum tax the source country can withhold under the treaty (domestic law may be lower; where the treaty rate is higher than domestic law, you pay the lower):

Income | Treaty article | Maximum source-country rate | 

Dividends — company holding at least 10% of voting stock | Article 10 | 15% | 

Dividends — all other cases | Article 10 | 25% | 

Interest — loans from banks / financial institutions | Article 11 | 10% | 

Interest — other cases | Article 11 | 15% | 

Royalties for use of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, and related services | Article 12 | 10% | 

Other royalties and fees for included services | Article 12 | 15% | 

Business profits without a permanent establishment in the other country | Article 7 | Not taxable in the source country | 

## Fees for services — the tricky one

The India–US treaty doesn’t tax every technical fee at source. “Fees for included services” covers services that are ancillary to a royalty, or that make available technical knowledge, skills, know-how or processes to the payer so they can use it themselves. Routine services that don’t transfer that capability — many consulting, marketing or support services — may instead be business profits, taxable in the source country only if there’s a permanent establishment. Getting this characterisation right is often the difference between 15% withholding and none.

## Claiming treaty rates

### When a US payer pays an Indian person or company

- Give the US payer Form W-8BEN-E (entities) or W-8BEN (individuals), claiming treaty benefits under the relevant article — see how to fill W-8BEN-E.

- Without it, US payers generally withhold at the full 30% statutory rate on US-source fixed income such as dividends or royalties.

### When an Indian payer pays a US person or company

- The US recipient provides a Tax Residency Certificate (for US residents, typically IRS Form 6166) and the self-declaration India requires (Form 41, formerly Form 10F, filed electronically).

- The Indian payer applies the lower of the domestic or treaty rate, and completes the remittance documentation with its bank and chartered accountant.

## Foreign tax credit in India

An Indian resident taxed in the US on income that India also taxes can claim a foreign tax credit in India, limited to the Indian tax on that income. The claim requires a prescribed statement, with your return filed on time:

- Form 67 for foreign income up to FY 2025-26 — by the end of the relevant assessment year.

- Form 44 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 for income from 1 April 2026 — within 12 months from the end of the tax year; a foreign tax identification number is mandatory.

Keep proof of US tax paid — US returns, withholding statements or Form 1042-S.

## 2026: India’s new Income-tax Act

From 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 and Income-tax Rules, 2026 replaced the 1961 Act, and many forms were renumbered. For cross-border payments this matters in practice: remittance documentation formerly done in Forms 15CA/15CB now uses Forms 145/146 for payments on or after 1 April 2026, and the transfer-pricing accountant’s report formerly in Form 3CEB is now Form 48. The India–US treaty itself is unchanged.

## Founder scenarios

- Your Delaware C-Corp pays you a dividend: US withholding applies (25% for an individual shareholder under the treaty, if you give a W-8BEN); you pay Indian tax on the dividend and claim credit for the US tax. See C-Corp vs LLC.

- Your Indian company sells software services to US clients: usually business profits taxable only in India if you have no US permanent establishment — give clients a W-8BEN-E.

- Your US subsidiary pays the Indian parent for development work: priced at arm’s length and documented for transfer pricing. See US subsidiary of an Indian company.

- You own a US LLC: the US may ignore the LLC while India treats it as a separate company, which can complicate treaty access and credits. See ODI & tax rules for US companies.

Are you the foreign side of the payment? Read Form 41, TRC and the no-PE declaration.
Living in the US? NRIs in the US: Indian tax, FBAR, FATCA & PFIC.

## Frequently asked questions
What is the dividend tax rate under the India–US DTAA?
The source country can tax dividends at up to 15% when the beneficial owner is a company holding at least 10% of the payer's voting stock, and up to 25% in other cases.

How do I claim India–US treaty rates on payments from US clients?
Provide the US payer with Form W-8BEN-E (for a company) or W-8BEN (for an individual) claiming the relevant treaty article. Without it, US payers generally withhold at 30% on fixed income such as dividends and royalties.

Which form is used to claim foreign tax credit in India?
Form 67 for foreign income up to FY 2025-26, and Form 44 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 for income from 1 April 2026. Form 44 can be filed within 12 months from the end of the tax year, provided the return was filed on time.

Did India's new Income-tax Act change the India–US DTAA?
No. The treaty is unchanged, but from 1 April 2026 Indian domestic forms were renumbered — for example Forms 145/146 replace 15CA/15CB and Form 48 replaces Form 3CEB.

Cross-border guide

# Delaware flip for Indian startups: should you set up a US holdco?

A Delaware parent can open doors to US capital and customers. It can also create tax and FEMA problems that take years to unwind. Here’s how to decide.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 6 October 2026·9 min read

Discuss your structure
hello@durgeshchavda.com

## What is a Delaware flip?

A flip moves an Indian startup under a US parent company, usually a Delaware C-Corp. The founders and existing investors end up holding shares in the US company, and the Indian company becomes its subsidiary — typically where the team, operations and costs remain.

## Why founders flip

- Investor preference — many US funds and accelerators invest only in Delaware companies with standard documents.

- US customers and credibility — contracting with enterprise customers as a US entity.

- US hiring — stock options that US employees understand.

- Exit path — US acquirers and listing options.

If most of your capital, customers and future exit are in India, those advantages shrink — and the costs remain.

## How a flip works: the three routes

Route | How it works | Where it gets hard | 

Fresh US parent + migration | Incorporate the Delaware parent, raise into it, set up or move operations to a subsidiary and migrate the business over time | Slower; IP and contracts must move cleanly; transfer pricing from day one | 

Share swap | Shareholders of the Indian company exchange their shares for shares of the Delaware company, which then owns the Indian company | FEMA: resident individuals can acquire foreign shares by swap only in limited cases, and an individual who controls a foreign company can’t have it own subsidiaries — so a plain founder swap usually doesn’t work on the automatic route. Taxable for resident shareholders. | 

Indian entity holds the US stake | Founders invest via an Indian company or LLP, which makes the overseas direct investment under the more flexible entity rules | Adds a layer; round-tripping rules limit structures to two layers of subsidiaries | 

## FEMA and overseas investment (ODI)

- Resident individuals can make overseas direct investment only in an operating foreign company not engaged in financial services — and if they control it (10% of voting rights through agreements can be enough), it can’t have subsidiaries or step-down subsidiaries. A founder-controlled Delaware parent owning the Indian company is exactly that structure.

- Swaps: resident individuals can acquire foreign shares by swap only in specified cases such as mergers, demergers or amalgamations; non-conforming holdings must be unwound.

- Round-tripping: a structure where a foreign company invests back into India can’t have more than two layers of subsidiaries.

- The Indian leg: since August 2024, India’s non-debt instrument rules expressly allow share swaps for non-residents acquiring Indian shares, with valuations on both legs and government approval where an investor is from a country sharing a land border with India.

### Filings

- Overseas investment by Indian residents: Form FC through the authorised dealer bank when the investment is made; an Annual Performance Report by 31 December every year.

- Indian shares moving to the US parent: FC-TRS within 60 days of the transfer or receipt of consideration, whichever is earlier.

- New shares issued by the Indian company to the parent: FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment; then the annual FLA return.

- Valuations on both legs — FEMA pricing for the Indian shares and, for swaps, a valuation by a SEBI-registered merchant banker (or an overseas regulated investment banker) for the foreign shares.

- Investors from countries sharing a land border with India (e.g. a Chinese shareholder) need government approval.

## Tax considerations

- Capital gains on the swap — for resident shareholders, exchanging Indian shares for foreign shares is generally a taxable transfer, with the gain driven by the valuation and holding period.

- POEM — if key management decisions of the US company are effectively taken in India, it risks being treated as tax-resident in India under the Place of Effective Management rules.

- Transfer pricing — the Indian subsidiary must be remunerated at arm’s length (commonly cost-plus) with documentation to match.

- US tax and compliance — federal corporate tax, Delaware franchise tax and annual report, and US reporting for foreign-owned or foreign-subsidiary structures.

- Withholding and DTAA — dividends, royalties and service fees between India and the US, and treaty relief.

## The reverse-flip trend

In recent years several well-known Indian startups have moved their holding companies back to India ahead of an Indian listing — often paying significant tax to do so. India has also eased the mechanics of inbound share swaps. The lesson: a flip is easy to start and expensive to reverse, so it should follow a clear strategic reason. How the return journey works: reverse flip to India.

## A simple decision test

Lean towards a US holdco if… | Lean towards staying Indian if… | 

Your lead investors require a Delaware entity | Most of your investors are India-focused funds | 

Most revenue comes from US customers | Customers and revenue are primarily in India | 

You expect a US acquisition or listing | An Indian IPO is a realistic outcome | 

Founders are, or will be, based in the US | Founders and management will stay in India | 

If you’re weighing it up, see our India–US flip service — or message Durgesh with your cap table and investor mix.

## Frequently asked questions
Is a Delaware flip still worth it for Indian startups?
It depends on your investors, customers, founder location and exit path. It is most useful when US investors require it and the business is US-facing; for India-focused companies an Indian parent is often simpler and avoids reverse-flip costs later.

Is the share swap in a Delaware flip taxable in India?
Generally yes for resident shareholders — the exchange is treated as a transfer and can create capital-gains tax, based on valuation and holding period.

What is POEM and why does it matter for a flip?
POEM (Place of Effective Management) tests where key management and commercial decisions are actually made. If a US parent is effectively run from India, it may be treated as an Indian tax resident.

Which FEMA rules apply to a Delaware flip?
Resident shareholders acquiring the US parent's shares fall under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, while the US parent's holding in the Indian company is foreign investment reported under FEMA non-debt instrument rules (e.g., FC-TRS / FC-GPR).

Can a resident Indian founder simply swap shares into a Delaware company?
Usually not on the automatic route. Resident individuals can acquire foreign shares by swap only in specified cases, and an individual who controls a foreign company cannot have it own subsidiaries under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022 — so the flip has to be structured differently, for example through a fresh parent with migration or an Indian entity holding the US stake.

Deadline 31 December 2026

# FAST-DS 2026: clean up undisclosed foreign assets by 31 December

Foreign bank accounts, RSUs and ESOPs from a US or UK employer, a dormant account from student days — India’s tax department now sees them through global data exchange. FAST-DS is a one-time window to put them right at a known cost.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 4 November 2026·5 min read

Get your disclosure reviewed
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Got the email about “overseas financial interests”? What the FAST-DS email means and what to do.
Closes 31 December 2026. No declaration can be filed after that date. We handle the valuation and the filing end to end.WhatsApp usFree 15-min callHow we file

## What FAST-DS is

The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (Chapter IV of the Finance Act, 2026; rules notified on 14 August 2026) is a one-time window to declare foreign assets and income that were never reported in India, at a fixed cost and with immunity under the Black Money Act. It opened on 16 August 2026 and closes on 31 December 2026. Values are taken as on 31 March 2026.

Why now: foreign account data received under CRS and FATCA is showing up against PANs, and many taxpayers are getting messages about foreign assets missing from Schedule FA.

## Who can use it

- Anyone who was resident in India in the year the foreign income arose or the foreign asset was acquired.

- That includes people who are NRIs or RNORs today: you state your residential status for the relevant year in Form 1.

- It covers cases where you did not file a return, filed but left the asset or income out, or the income escaped assessment.

- Not available for proceeds of crime where money-laundering proceedings have started, or for years already assessed under the Black Money Act.

## The two categories

| Category 1: undisclosed | Category 2: not reported | 

What it covers | A foreign asset whose source you cannot explain, or foreign income that was taxable in India but never offered to tax | A foreign asset bought from income already taxed, or bought while you were a non-resident, but left out of Schedule FA | 

Limit | Asset value plus income up to ₹1 crore in aggregate | Asset value up to ₹5 crore in aggregate | 

Cost | 30% tax plus an equal amount: 60% | Flat ₹1,00,000 | 

Typical case | Unreported foreign rent, dividends, interest or sale gains while resident; an account funded from money that escaped Indian tax | RSUs taxed through Indian payroll; savings from years abroad; a student-days account | 

Worked example (from the department’s FAQs): a foreign bank account worth ₹60 lakh and ₹20 lakh of undisclosed foreign income. Tax at 30% is ₹18 lakh plus ₹6 lakh, plus an equal additional amount, so ₹48 lakh in all.

Try your numbers in the FAST-DS calculator.

## How assets are valued (as on 31 March 2026)

Asset | Value | 

Bank account | Sum of all deposits since the account was opened, not the balance (deposits made out of withdrawals from the same account are excluded) | 

Listed shares, including RSUs and ESPP shares | Higher of cost and the average of the highest and lowest price on 31 March 2026 (or the nearest earlier trading day) | 

Unlisted shares and interests | Higher of cost and the value under the prescribed formula or a valuer’s report | 

Property | Higher of cost and market value, with a valuation report from a valuer recognised in that country | 

Jewellery, art, other assets | Higher of cost and market value | 

Foreign currency converts at the RBI reference rate on 31 March 2026 (other currencies go through US dollars first).

## How it works: Forms 1 to 4

- Form 1: the declaration, filed online with evidence of each asset and its value.

- Form 2: the department’s order stating the amount payable.

- Payment through challan ITNS 289 (assessment year 2026-27 is pre-filled; a wrong minor head cannot be corrected or refunded) within two months from the end of the month you receive Form 2. Up to two more months are allowed with 1% a month interest; after that the declaration is void.

- Form 3: intimation of payment with the proof.

- Form 4: the certificate confirming the payment.

## FAST-DS or wait and see?

If the department finds it first (Black Money Act) | If you declare it under FAST-DS | 

Undisclosed asset or income: tax at 30% plus a penalty of three times the tax, so 120% of the value, and possible prosecution | Category 1: 60%, with immunity under the Black Money Act | 

Asset only missing from Schedule FA: penalty of ₹10 lakh (not applied since 1 October 2024 where your foreign assets other than immovable property total ₹20 lakh or less) | Category 2: ₹1 lakh, with immunity | 

For small, already-taxed holdings under ₹20 lakh, FAST-DS may not be necessary: report them correctly in Schedule FA from now on. For anything larger, or anything with unreported income, FAST-DS is far cheaper than being found later.

## Common situations

- RSUs or ESPP shares from a foreign employer: FAST-DS for RSUs and ESOPs.

- A foreign bank account left open after studies or work: FAST-DS for foreign bank accounts.

- Back in India after years abroad: FAST-DS for returning NRIs.

Want it done for you? See our FAST-DS filing service.
Living abroad now? FAST-DS for NRIs in the UK, US, Canada and Australia.

## Frequently asked questions
What is FAST-DS 2026?
The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026: a one-time window, open from 16 August to 31 December 2026, to declare undisclosed foreign assets or income, or foreign assets left out of Schedule FA, at a fixed cost and with immunity under the Black Money Act.

What is the last date for FAST-DS 2026?
31 December 2026. No declaration can be filed after that date.

How much do you pay under FAST-DS?
For undisclosed foreign assets or income up to ₹1 crore in total: 30% tax plus an equal additional amount, 60% in all. For foreign assets from taxed income or acquired while non-resident, missing only from Schedule FA, up to ₹5 crore: a flat ₹1 lakh.

Can NRIs use FAST-DS?
Yes, if they were resident in India in the year the foreign asset was acquired or the foreign income arose, even if they are non-resident now.

What happens if my foreign assets are worth more than ₹5 crore?
You are not eligible for FAST-DS. Get specific advice on the Black Money Act position.

How is a foreign bank account valued for FAST-DS?
At the total of all deposits made since the account was opened, up to 31 March 2026, excluding deposits made out of withdrawals from the same account. It is not the account balance.

When do I pay after filing FAST-DS?
Within two months from the end of the month in which you receive the Form 2 order. A further two months is allowed with interest at 1% a month; after that the declaration is void.

Does FAST-DS give immunity?
A valid declaration with full payment gives immunity from further tax, penalty and prosecution under the Black Money Act for the assets and income declared.

NRI update

# The US 1% remittance tax — and how NRIs avoid paying it

Since 1 January 2026 the US has taxed some money sent abroad. For most NRIs sending money to India the answer is simple: fund the transfer from a bank account or a US card and the tax doesn’t apply.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Ask about NRI money transfers
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- The 1% US tax applies only to transfers funded with cash, money orders or cashier's checks, from 1 January 2026.
- Transfers from a US bank account or with a US debit/credit card are exempt.
- Nothing changes in India — money sent home by an NRI isn't taxable income there.

## What the tax is

- A 1% excise tax on remittance transfers made after 31 December 2025, under section 4475 of the US Internal Revenue Code (enacted in 2025).

- The sender bears it; the money-transfer provider collects it and pays it to the IRS.

- It applies to everyone sending, not only non-citizens.

## Which transfers are taxed — and which aren’t

How you fund the transfer | 1% tax? | 

Cash at a counter | Yes | 

Money order, cashier’s check or similar physical instrument | Yes | 

From your US bank or credit-union account (online transfer, wire, app linked to your account) | No | 

US-issued debit or credit card | No | 

Proposed IRS regulations (April 2026) treat cashed-check proceeds as cash and include anti-avoidance rules; very small transfers excluded under existing remittance rules stay outside. Final regulations were not yet out at the time of writing.

## The India side doesn’t change

- Money an NRI sends home isn’t income in India — no Indian tax on receiving it.

- Gifts to relatives are tax-free in India; gifts to non-relatives above ₹50,000 can be taxable for the recipient.

- Investing in India? Route money through an NRE account so it stays fully repatriable.

- Sending money out of India is a different matter — Indian TCS on remittances: TCS on foreign remittance.

## Sources

- KPMG — proposed regulations on the remittance excise tax (Apr 2026)
Sending money between India and your country? Limits, forms and local tax rules.

## Frequently asked questions
Does the US 1% remittance tax apply to bank transfers to India?
No. Transfers funded from a US bank or credit-union account, and transfers paid with a US-issued debit or credit card, are excluded. The tax applies to transfers funded with cash, money orders, cashier's checks and similar physical instruments.

When did the US remittance tax start?
It applies to remittance transfers made after 31 December 2025.

Who pays the US remittance tax?
The sender. The remittance transfer provider collects it and pays it to the IRS, and is liable if it fails to collect.

Is money received from abroad taxed in India?
Money an NRI sends to family isn't taxable income in India. Gifts from relatives are exempt; gifts above ₹50,000 from non-relatives can be taxable for the person receiving them.

Property guide

# Can foreigners buy property in India? It depends who you are

India’s foreign-exchange rules treat foreign nationals, Overseas Citizens of India and NRIs very differently when it comes to property. Here’s the rule for each — and how money gets back out.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Ask about Indian property
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Foreign nationals (non-OCI) can't buy Indian property — only inherit it or lease up to 5 years.
- NRIs and OCIs can buy homes and commercial property, but not agricultural land.
- NRIs and OCIs can repatriate up to USD 1 million a year from NRO accounts after tax.

## Who can buy what

You are | Homes & commercial property | Agricultural land, plantations, farmhouses | 

NRI (Indian citizen abroad) | Yes — buy freely | No (inheritance only) | 

OCI cardholder | Yes — buy freely | No (inheritance only) | 

Foreign national living outside India (not OCI) | No — only by inheritance from a person resident in India; leases up to 5 years allowed | No | 

Citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal or Bhutan (not OCI) | Needs prior RBI permission, wherever resident (except leases up to 5 years) | No | 

A foreign company can hold property in India through an Indian subsidiary for its business, or through a branch office for permitted activities — see doing business in India.

## How NRIs and OCIs pay

- Only through normal banking channels — inward remittance or NRE / NRO / FCNR accounts. No payment in foreign currency to the seller in India.

- Home loans from Indian banks are available to NRIs and OCIs.

## Tax while you own it and when you sell

- Rent is taxable in India, with TDS deducted by the tenant.

- On sale, the buyer deducts TDS — often far more than the final tax; a lower-deduction certificate (Form 128) helps. Since 1 October 2026, resident individual and HUF buyers can deposit this TDS using their PAN through Form 141, without getting a TAN. See TDS on property sale by an NRI and the capital gains calculator.

## Taking the money out

- Sale proceeds of up to two residential properties bought with foreign money can be repatriated under the rules.

- Otherwise NRIs and OCIs can repatriate up to USD 1 million per financial year from their NRO account after tax, with Forms 145 and 146 (formerly 15CA/15CB). See NRO repatriation.

## Sources

- RBI — FAQs on acquisition of immovable property by non-residents

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreigner buy property in India?
Generally no. A foreign national living outside India who is not an OCI can acquire Indian property only by inheritance from a person resident in India, though leases of up to five years are allowed. OCIs and NRIs can buy residential and commercial property.

Can OCI cardholders buy property in India?
Yes — residential and commercial property, freely. They cannot buy agricultural land, plantation property or farmhouses except by inheritance.

Can NRIs buy agricultural land in India?
No. NRIs and OCIs can't buy agricultural land, plantations or farmhouses; they can only inherit them.

How much money can an NRI repatriate from India?
Up to USD 1 million per financial year from the NRO account, after tax, supported by Forms 145 and 146; balances in NRE accounts are fully repatriable.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Investor guide

# How foreigners can invest in the Indian stock market

Until June 2026 a foreign national needed FPI registration to buy Indian shares. Not any more — a 2026 FEMA amendment opened the direct route NRIs use to every individual living outside India. Here are the routes, the limits and the tax.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 3 November 2026·6 min read

Plan your India investment
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Reporting under the June 2026 rules: RBI’s companion payment and reporting regulations require repatriable investments by foreign individuals in listed Indian shares to go through a designated repatriable rupee account, and introduce a new reporting form, Form LEC (IFI), handled through the authorised dealer bank. Each individual stays below 10% of a company’s paid-up equity, with an aggregate cap of 24% for such individuals.

Key takeaways
- Since 12 June 2026, any individual living outside India can buy listed Indian shares directly — no FPI registration.
- Each individual must stay below 10% of a company; all such individuals together below 24%.
- SWAGAT-FI (from 1 June 2026) eases registration for low-risk foreign investors.

## The three routes

Route | For | How | 

Direct route for individuals (new, June 2026) | Any individual resident outside India — foreign nationals, NRIs, OCIs | Indian broker and demat account with a designated bank account; holding must stay below 10% of a company (24% for all such individuals together) | 

Foreign portfolio investor (FPI) | Funds, family offices, companies — and individuals who prefer it | Register with SEBI through a designated custodian (individuals as Category II FPIs) | 

GIFT City (IFSC) funds | Foreign investors who prefer a fund | Invest in a fund set up in GIFT City that invests in India — see investing through GIFT City | 

Exceed 10% in a company and the excess must be sold within 5 trading days, or the whole holding is treated as FDI. Investors with beneficial owners in a country bordering India need government approval where ownership or control could pass to them.

Indirect exposure — India ETFs and ADRs listed abroad — needs no Indian registration at all.

## What changed in 2026

- FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Third Amendment Rules, 2026 (notified 12 June 2026): the listed-equity route that was open only to NRIs and OCIs now covers any individual resident outside India.

- SWAGAT-FI (SEBI circulars of January 2026, effective 1 June 2026): faster single-window registration and longer validity for low-risk FPIs such as government funds, regulated retail funds, insurers and pension funds.

- NRIs, OCIs and resident Indians can contribute up to 100% of an IFSC-based FPI (in place since 2024).

## Tax on gains

- Listed equity: long-term gains (held over 12 months) 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh; short-term 20% — treaty relief may apply.

- Dividends are taxed in India, with treaty rates available — see dividend withholding by country.

- FPIs need a PAN and usually a local tax representative.

## Sources

- India Briefing — FEMA non-debt amendment for foreign individuals (2026)
- Taxscan — FEMA NDI rules opened to all individuals resident outside India
- SEBI — SWAGAT-FI circular (Jan 2026)
Related: the reverse: Indians investing in US stocks · tax on IPO gains.

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreigner invest in the Indian stock market?
Yes. Since 12 June 2026 any individual resident outside India can buy listed Indian shares directly through an Indian broker and demat account, without FPI registration, as long as each holding stays below 10% of the company. Funds and companies use FPI registration or GIFT City funds.

Can a US citizen buy Indian stocks directly?
Yes, since the FEMA amendment of 12 June 2026, through an Indian broker and demat account with a designated bank account, subject to the below-10% per-company limit — though some Indian brokers restrict US residents, so check before opening an account.

Can a foreign individual register as an FPI in India?
Yes. Individuals can register as Category II FPIs with SEBI through a designated custodian, subject to KYC requirements.

What is SWAGAT-FI?
A SEBI framework effective 1 June 2026 that gives low-risk foreign investors — such as government funds, regulated retail funds, insurers and pension funds — single-window registration with longer validity.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

# Can NRIs apply for IPOs in India? Yes — here’s how

Jio Platforms’ IPO closed for bidding on 23 October 2026, with allotment due on 26 October and listing on 28 October. Here’s how NRIs apply in Indian IPOs, what happens after bidding closes, and the tax.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 28 October 2026·6 min read

Plan your IPO investment
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Booked a gain this year? Get your capital gains and income tax return handled by a Chartered Accountant. Ask on WhatsApp (first 10 messages free) or book a 30-minute call for ₹499.Ask on WhatsAppBook a call

Free tool: IPO tax calculator: enter your allotment price, selling price and shares to see your exact tax.

Quick answers
- Can NRIs apply for IPOs in India? Yes — through ASBA from an NRE or NRO account, holding the shares in an NRI demat account.
- NRE keeps proceeds fully repatriable; NRO is limited to USD 1 million a year.
- Always check the issue’s red herring prospectus for NRI eligibility and category.
- Tax: 20% if sold within 12 months; 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh after — details.

Key takeaways
- NRIs can apply in Indian IPOs via ASBA from an NRE or NRO account with an NRI demat account.
- NRE keeps proceeds fully repatriable; NRO is limited to USD 1 million a year.
- Jio Platforms' IPO closed on 23 October 2026; allotment is due on 26 October and listing on 28 October (tentative).

Got Jio Platforms shares? Worked tax examples at the ₹1,358 listing price.

## How NRIs apply

- Apply through ASBA (net banking or your broker’s UPI/ASBA flow) from an NRE or NRO account.

- Hold the shares in an NRI demat account linked to the same type of account (repatriable or non-repatriable).

- A PIS permission is generally not needed for IPO applications; some brokers restrict US and Canadian residents — check before applying.

- Always check the offer document (RHP) for whether NRIs are eligible in that issue and in which category.

## NRE or NRO?

- NRE (repatriable): invest with money from abroad; sale proceeds can go back out freely after tax.

- NRO (non-repatriable): use Indian income; proceeds stay within the USD 1 million-a-year repatriation limit.

- More: NRE vs NRO vs FCNR.

## Tax on IPO gains

Sell within 12 months: 20% short-term capital gains. After 12 months: 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh. Brokers deduct TDS for NRIs; treaty relief and credits at home may apply. Details: tax on IPO listing gains.

## Big IPOs to watch

- Jio Platforms: a fresh issue of 27 crore shares. Its red herring prospectus (14 October 2026) sets a price band of ₹1,065–1,119 and a lot of 12 shares; bidding runs 21–23 October 2026 after an anchor book of about ₹8,110 crore, with listing expected around 28 October. Check the RHP for NRI eligibility.

- NSE listed on 24 September 2026.

- PhonePe: approved by SEBI; launch postponed, no date set.

## Sources

- Kotak Neo — Jio Platforms IPO expected price band
- Zerodha support — NRI IPO applications
Related: moving back to India.
Jio Platforms IPO closed 23 October 2026: subscribed about 22.19 times overall, per NSE data at 7 pm — qualified institutions about 70.5x, non-institutional investors about 14x and retail about 2.7x (Upstox). With retail oversubscribed, retail allotment is by lottery — many applicants will get no shares and their blocked money is released.
Jio Platforms listed on 28 October 2026 at ₹1,358 on NSE and BSE, a 21.36% premium to the ₹1,119 issue price (lot of 12 shares). If you sold at the listing price, the gain is ₹239 a share, or ₹2,868 per lot. That is a short-term gain taxed at 20% plus 4% cess (plus surcharge where applicable): about ₹597 per lot before surcharge. Hold beyond 12 months and gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year are taxed at 12.5%. NRIs: the broker deducts TDS. See NRIs in IPOs. Listing price as reported by Groww, Upstox and National Herald; your actual sale price sets your gain.

## After bidding closes: allotment, refunds and listing

Step | Jio Platforms timetable (as reported) | What NRIs should do | 

Allotment | 26 October 2026 | Check status on the registrar’s site or the exchange website with your PAN or application number. | 

Funds unblocked / shares credited | 27 October 2026 | Confirm the ASBA block on your NRE or NRO account is released for any shares not allotted, and that allotted shares reach your NRI demat account. | 

Listing | 28 October 2026 (tentative) | Decide whether to hold or sell. Selling within 12 months is short-term — tax at 20%, deducted by the broker for NRIs. | 

- Oversubscribed issues allot retail shares by lottery, so many applicants receive none — the blocked money is simply released.

- Proceeds go back to the account you applied from: NRE (fully repatriable) or NRO (repatriation within the USD 1 million a year limit, with Forms 145/146 where needed).

- File an Indian return if TDS was deducted on your gains and you want any excess back, or if the treaty with your country of residence gives a lower rate — see tax on IPO gains.

## Frequently asked questions
How many times was the Jio Platforms IPO subscribed?
About 22.19 times overall when bidding closed on 23 October 2026, per NSE data at 7 pm — around 70.5 times in the qualified institutional portion, 14 times for non-institutional investors and 2.7 times for retail.

When is the Jio Platforms IPO allotment and listing?
As reported from the issue timetable: allotment on 26 October 2026, unblocking of funds and credit of shares on 27 October, and listing on BSE and NSE on 28 October 2026 (tentative). Check status on the registrar's or exchange's website.

Can NRIs apply for the Jio Platforms IPO?
NRIs can generally apply in Indian IPOs through ASBA from an NRE or NRO account; whether and in which category NRIs could bid in a specific issue is set out in its red herring prospectus.

Can NRIs apply for IPOs in India?
Yes. NRIs apply through ASBA from an NRE or NRO bank account and hold allotted shares in an NRI demat account; check the offer document for NRI eligibility in each issue.

Should NRIs use NRE or NRO for IPO investment?
Use NRE for money brought from abroad if you want proceeds to be freely repatriable; NRO for Indian income, with repatriation within the USD 1 million-a-year limit.

How are NRI IPO gains taxed?
Shares sold within 12 months: 20% short-term gains; after 12 months: 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year. TDS is deducted, and a return can recover any excess.

Trade deal update

# India–UK trade deal in force: what changes for businesses

The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement took effect on 15 July 2026, alongside a social-security deal that matters to every company sending staff between the two countries.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 25 October 2026·5 min read

Talk about India–UK business
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- The India–UK CETA took effect on 15 July 2026.
- The Double Contributions Convention spares posted employees double social-security contributions for up to 5 years.
- Income tax still follows the India–UK tax treaty.

Three months in (October 2026): on 13 October the UK held its first CETA Marketplace in Mumbai — one of its largest business delegations to India, with around 200 UK businesses across advanced manufacturing, clean tech, healthcare, fintech, education, consumer products and infrastructure (report). For UK firms, the next step after a marketplace meeting is checking the Indian partner — see due diligence for UK companies.

## What happened

- CETA was signed on 24 July 2025 and took effect on 15 July 2026.

- The Double Contributions Convention (DCC), signed on 10 February 2026, took effect the same day.

## The social-security win: no double contributions

- Employees temporarily posted from India to the UK (or the UK to India) can stay in their home social-security system for up to 5 years (60 months), instead of paying into both.

- It covers employees, not the self-employed. Get the certificate of coverage before the posting starts.

- For Indian IT and services companies with UK projects, and UK firms with India teams, this is a direct cost saving.

## Goods and services

- Tariffs on most Indian exports to the UK are removed or cut; UK goods such as whisky, cars and medical devices get phased tariff cuts into India.

- Rules of origin decide who benefits — exporters need origin certificates and records.

## What doesn’t change

Income tax between India and the UK is still governed by the India–UK tax treaty: withholding on dividends, royalties and fees, and permanent-establishment rules. See India–UK cross-border services and India tax for foreign companies.

## Sources

- Chambers — India-UK CETA in force
- AccountingWEB — UK-India double contributions
UK group with India operations? Failure to prevent fraud: what it means for your India operations.

## Frequently asked questions
Is the India–UK trade deal in force?
Yes. The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement took effect on 15 July 2026, after being signed on 24 July 2025.

What is the India–UK Double Contributions Convention?
A social-security agreement in force from 15 July 2026 that lets employees temporarily posted between India and the UK stay in their home system for up to five years instead of paying contributions in both countries.

Does the India–UK trade deal change income tax?
No. Income tax is still governed by the India–UK tax treaty; CETA covers tariffs, services and investment, and the DCC covers social-security contributions.

US companies

# The H-1B fee fight — and the India option

Whatever happens to the $100,000 H-1B fee in court, US companies are rethinking where engineering and operations work gets done. Here’s the status, and the three ways to build a team in India.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·5 min read

Plan your India team
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- A US court vacated the $100,000 H-1B fee in June 2026; it isn't being collected, but the legal fight continues.
- US companies can build in India through a vendor, an employer of record or their own subsidiary (GCC).
- A cost-plus Indian subsidiary is the usual long-term structure.

## Where the fee stands (October 2026)

- A September 2025 proclamation imposed a $100,000 payment on new H-1B petitions for workers outside the US.

- In June 2026 a federal court in Massachusetts held the fee unlawful and vacated it; the appeals court refused to pause that ruling in July, and the fee has not been collected since.

- Another court upheld the fee in December 2025, and a new proclamation in September 2026 extended it to September 2027 — so the legal position is unsettled. Check with immigration counsel before relying on either outcome.

## Three ways to build in India

Option | Speed | Control | Best for | 

Outsourcing / vendor | Fast | Low | Defined projects | 

Employer of record | 1–2 weeks | Medium | First 5–10 hires | 

Own subsidiary (GCC) | 1–2 months | High | Long-term teams | 

Compare them: hiring without an entity · setting up a GCC · India entry structure chooser.

## Tax and cost points

- A subsidiary billing the US parent cost plus a markup; eligible IT and ITeS units can use the safe-harbour option under India’s Income-tax Rules, 2026.

- Services exported to the parent can be zero-rated for GST.

- Staff without an entity can create permanent-establishment risk — plan before hiring.

## Sources

- Mintz — H-1B fee extension (Sep 2026)
- Fragomen — H-1B proclamation updates

## Frequently asked questions
Is the $100,000 H-1B fee still in effect?
As of October 2026 it is not being collected: a federal court vacated it in June 2026 and the appeals court refused to stay that ruling. But another court upheld it and a new proclamation extended it to 2027, so the position is unsettled — check with immigration counsel.

How can a US company build a team in India?
Through an outsourcing vendor, an employer of record for the first hires, or its own Indian subsidiary (often called a GCC) charging the parent cost plus a markup.

Is a GCC in India tax-efficient for a US company?
It is taxed in India on its markup, usually at a 22% base rate option, and services to the parent can be zero-rated for GST; transfer-pricing documentation is essential.

Hiring guide

# Paying Indian freelancers from abroad — both sides explained

Foreign companies hire Indian designers, developers and consultants every day. The good news: the foreign client’s obligations are light. The Indian freelancer has a few things to get right.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 15 October 2026·6 min read

Ask about freelancer tax
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Foreign clients without an Indian presence generally have no Indian tax to withhold.
- Indian freelancers' services to foreign clients are zero-rated exports for GST with an LUT.
- Specified professionals can use presumptive tax under section 58 (50% of receipts).

## If you’re the foreign client

- Generally no Indian tax to withhold when a foreign company with no Indian presence pays an Indian resident freelancer.

- Pay through banking channels so the freelancer receives a foreign-inward-remittance advice (e-FIRA) — their proof of export.

- Keep it a genuine contractor relationship. Full-time, directed “freelancers” can create employment and permanent-establishment risk.

- Collect your own country’s forms (e.g. W-8BEN in the US) as your home rules require.

## If you’re the Indian freelancer

- GST: services to a foreign client paid in foreign currency are an export — zero-rated. Register once turnover crosses ₹20 lakh, file a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) each year and invoice without IGST. See GST on export of services.

- Income tax: specified professionals (engineering, technical consultancy, accountancy, legal, architecture, interior decoration and notified professions) can use the presumptive scheme under section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 — 50% of receipts taxed, up to ₹75 lakh where cash receipts are 5% or less. Others are taxed on actual profit.

- Advance tax applies — see the advance tax guide.

## Sources

- Income-tax e-filing portal
- GST portal

## Frequently asked questions
Does a foreign company have to deduct tax when paying an Indian freelancer?
Generally no, where the foreign company has no presence in India. It should pay through banking channels so the freelancer gets an e-FIRA as proof of the export.

Do Indian freelancers charge GST to foreign clients?
No GST is charged when the service qualifies as an export — foreign client, payment in foreign currency. Registered freelancers file an LUT and invoice at zero rate.

Can Indian freelancers use presumptive taxation?
Specified professionals can, under section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025: 50% of receipts is treated as income, up to ₹75 lakh of receipts where cash receipts are 5% or less.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.
